title: BUG: str.get_dummies misinterprets literal separators on object dtype
body:
Update after triage: This issue has been reclassified as a bug. The planned fix is to treat the separator literally in the object implementation, matching the Arrow implementation, without adding a public regex parameter.

PR #70812 will be revised accordingly. The original proposal below is retained for context; its proposed API change has been superseded by this approach.

### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

> I would like to use Series.str.get_dummies with a literal separator that contains spaces and a pipe, without preprocessing the input strings.
>
> For example:
>
> ```python
> import pandas as pd
>
> s = pd.Series(
>     ["Remote | On site", "Remote", "On site"],
>     dtype=object,
> )
>
> print(s.str.get_dummies(sep=" | ").to_dict(orient="list"))
> ```
>
> On pandas 3.0.6, this produces:
>
> ```python
> {
>     "On": [0, 0, 0],
>     "Remote": [1, 1, 0],
>     "site": [0, 0, 0],
>     "|": [0, 0, 0],
> }
> ```
>
> The separator is not treated literally, multi-word category names are split, and the indicator values are incorrect.
>
> There is currently no regex=False argument that would let callers request literal separator handling directly.

### Feature Description

> Add a keyword-only regex parameter to Series.str.get_dummies:
>
> ```python
> def get_dummies(self, sep="|", dtype=None, *, regex=True):
>     ...
> ```
>
> Proposed behavior:
>
> - regex=False: always interpret sep as a literal string.
> - regex=True, or omitting the argument: preserve the existing separator handling and results.
>
> The new literal mode would allow:
>
> ```python
> s.str.get_dummies(sep=" | ", regex=False)
> ```
>
> Expected result:
>
> ```python
> {
>     "On site": [1, 0, 1],
>     "Remote": [1, 1, 0],
> }
> ```
>
> Compatibility is a requirement of this proposal. Existing calls should retain their behavior, including calls using the default single-character separator "|".
>
> In particular, regex=True would be a compatibility setting here. It should not be forwarded directly as regex=True to str.split, because the existing Python implementation uses str.split's default regex=None behavior. The existing Arrow implementation also needs to retain its current behavior.
>
> This proposal adds an explicit literal mode. It does not attempt to redesign or expand regular-expression support in the existing default mode.
>
> Tests should cover literal separators with regex metacharacters, multi-word labels, existing default behavior, string backends, and Index.str.get_dummies.

### Alternative Solutions

> For consistently formatted input, a workaround is to replace the separator before encoding:
>
> ```python
> s.str.replace(" | ", "|", regex=False).str.get_dummies(sep="|")
> ```
>
> This requires an extra preprocessing step and changes the input representation solely to work around separator interpretation.
>
> An explicit regex=False argument would make the intended behavior directly expressible in get_dummies while preserving existing behavior for callers who do not opt in.

### Additional Context

> A local prototype adds the parameter, forwards it through the relevant implementations, and uses literal splitting only when regex=False. The default path preserves existing behavior.
>
> The prototype also includes regression tests and documentation explaining the compatibility semantics of regex=True.

title: BUG: str.replace/contains/match/count with \w, \d, \s, \b only match ASCII for default str dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ser = pd.Series(["café crème!", "Müller-Lüdenscheidt", "東京 2024"])
print(ser.str.replace(r"[^\w\s]", "", regex=True).tolist())
# ['caf crme', 'MllerLdenscheidt', ' 2024']

print(ser.astype(object).str.replace(r"[^\w\s]", "", regex=True).tolist())
# ['café crème', 'MüllerLüdenscheidt', '東京 2024']

print(pd.Series(["naïve"]).str.fullmatch(r"\w+")[0])
# False  (True with object dtype)
```

### Issue Description

What goes wrong:
With the default string dtype, regex character classes like \w, \d, \s, and \b behave as ASCII-only. As a result, accented and other non-English characters can be incorrectly treated as non-word characters.

Which methods are affected:
The issue affects str.replace, str.contains, str.match, str.fullmatch, and str.count. Object dtype and pandas 2 behavior are Unicode-aware.

Why it matters:
This can cause silent data changes or corruption in common text-cleaning workflows when users upgrade, especially for datasets containing international or accented text.

Cause:
These string operations are routed through PyArrow/RE2, where these regex character classes are ASCII-only. The issue is related to #63683, but that issue does not explicitly cover this case.

Fix ready:
I already have a proposed fix with tests and can open a PR once the issue is triaged and confirmed.

AI disclosure:
I used Claude Code with claude-opus-5-5 at medium effort to help identify the bug, investigate the behavior, and prepare the fix and tests.


### Expected Behavior

Regex character classes such as \w, \d, \s, and \b should handle Unicode characters consistently with object dtype, including accented and non-English letters.

['café crème', 'MüllerLüdenscheidt', '東京 2024']

title: BUG: describe() raises for numeric ExtensionArrays whose scalars can't be cast to float (e.g. pint-pandas)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas (3.0.1).
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas (the relevant code in `pandas/core/methods/describe.py` is unchanged on main).

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import pint_pandas  # registers the "pint[...]" ExtensionDtype

s = pd.Series([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype="pint[m]")
s.describe()
```

```
pint.errors.DimensionalityError: Cannot convert from 'meter' to 'dimensionless'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:
...
  File ".../pandas/core/methods/describe.py", line 267, in describe_numeric_1d
    return Series(d, index=stat_index, name=series.name, dtype=dtype)
  ...
  File ".../pandas/core/arrays/numeric.py", line 164, in _coerce_to_data_and_mask
    values = np.asarray(values)
ValueError: setting an array element with a sequence.
```

`DataFrame.describe()` fails the same way for any frame with a pint column.

### Issue Description

`describe_numeric_1d` collects `[count, mean, std, min, *quantiles, max]` and then forces the result dtype. Every non-Arrow `ExtensionDtype` gets `Float64Dtype()` (added for GH#48340 / GH#48778):

```python
if isinstance(series.dtype, ExtensionDtype):
    if isinstance(series.dtype, ArrowDtype):
        ...
    else:
        dtype = Float64Dtype()
```

That fits the masked numeric dtypes (`Int64`, `Float32`, …). It doesn't fit third-party numeric EAs whose reductions return non-float scalars. For pint-pandas, `mean`, `std`, `min` and so on return `pint.Quantity` objects, and `count` is a plain int. pint refuses to convert a Quantity with units to a bare float, so `describe()` raises. Stripping the units to make the cast succeed would silently lose information.

pandas already has a carve-out for the same situation: Arrow timedeltas use `dtype=None` and so get object output (GH#53001).

### Expected Behavior

`describe()` should return a result instead of raising. For example, with `dtype=None` in `describe_numeric_1d` the result would be:

```
count            3
mean     2.0 meter
std      1.0 meter
min      1.0 meter
25%      1.5 meter
50%      2.0 meter
75%      2.5 meter
max      3.0 meter
dtype: object
```

Possible fixes:

1. Use `Float64Dtype()` only for `BaseMaskedDtype`, and `dtype=None` (inference, so object here) for other extension dtypes.
2. Try `Float64Dtype()` and fall back to `dtype=None` if the cast fails.
3. Let the dtype choose: add an `ExtensionDtype` hook for the describe result dtype, defaulting to option 1's behaviour.

I'm happy to open a PR for option 1 (or whichever approach is preferred).

title: BUG: DataFrame.all/any(skipna=False) raises TypeError for bool[pyarrow] column with NA
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.array([True, None], dtype="bool[pyarrow]")})

print(df["a"].all(skipna=False))  # <NA>
print(df.all(skipna=False))       # TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous
```

### Issue Description

1) On a single column all(skipna=False) returns <NA>, but on the DataFrame it raises TypeError.
2) It also happens with any, with axis=None, and with other Arrow types like int64[pyarrow].
3) Why: DataFrame._reduce converts results to numpy bool, and only skips that for the "boolean" dtype, so bool[pyarrow] results that contain NA can't be converted.
4) It's the Arrow version of #65710, which fixed the same crash for numpy-nullable dtypes.
5) The disclosure: Used Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, medium effort) to help find the bug and prepare a fix.

title: BUG: Series.mode(dropna=False) raises TypeError for nullable boolean dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([True, False, None], dtype="boolean")
print(s.mode(dropna=False))
```

### Issue Description

I get a TypeError when I call mode(dropna=False) on a nullable boolean Series containing a missing value. The same operation works with an Int64 Series.

The error starts with:
TypeError: values should be boolean numpy array

It looks like the boolean values are converted to numbers for counting, but one return path does not convert them back to booleans before building the result.

I have a local fix that restores the original data type before returning the result, and I would like to submit a pull request.



### Expected Behavior

I expect the result to contain False, True, and <NA>, since each appears once. The result should keep the boolean dtype without raising an error.

Expected output:

0    False
1     True
2     <NA>
dtype: boolean

title: DOC: Fix docs signature for various offset constructors
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

Multiple offset classes in pandas.tseries.offsets.
Examples:

- BusinessDay — constructor signature is displayed correctly: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.tseries.offsets.BusinessDay.html
- MonthBegin — constructor parameters are missing from the signature: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.tseries.offsets.MonthBegin.html
- BYearBegin — constructor parameters are missing from the signature: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.tseries.offsets.BYearBegin.html

### Documentation problem

Several offset classes do not show their constructor parameters at the top of the API page.
For example, BusinessDay shows a complete signature such as

`BusinessDay(n=1, normalize=False, offset=timedelta(0))`

while other offset classes only show the class name, although their constructors accept additional parameters.

### Suggested fix for documentation

The constructor signatures should be added to doc/source/signature_overrides.py.
For an example, see the fix for `BusinessHour` https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/70401 and the related PR #66461

For each class:
1. Check the constructor parameters and add missing parameters to `_OFFSET_PARAMETERS`, if needed.
2. Add the class and its parameters to `_OFFSET_SIGNATURES`.
3. Build the documentation locally.
4. Check the generated HTML page and verify that the full constructor signature, including parameter defaults, is correct.

Please comment here which the classes you'll work on before starting so we don't duplicate work. Prefer one or two related classes per PR.
No need to ask for permission to work on this, and no need to comment "take" as multiple people can work on this concurrently.

title: DEPR: setting a 2-D value into a single row (df.iloc[1] = np.array([[1, 2]]))
body:
```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
df.iloc[1] = np.array([[10, 11]])  # works: row 1 becomes [10, 11]
```

I'd expect this to raise: a scalar row key selects a 1-D row, and the value is 2-D. It works on numpy-backed frames only because numpy broadcasting drops the leading length-1 axis. Nothing in pandas supports it on purpose, and no test covers it. It already raises for EA (`Int64`) and datetime64 columns, and for the list spelling `[[10, 11]]` on numeric frames. `df.iloc[1] = one_row_df` also works, while the `.loc` equivalent raises.

The bigger problem: under a scalar row key, a nested value is ambiguous between "a 1×N row" and "one nested value per (object) cell", and the answer depends on block layout. With object columns `a` and `b`, `df.loc[0, ["a", "b"]] = value` gives:

| value | single object block | object `a`, `b` + an int column |
|---|---|---|
| `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]` | `[1, 2]`, `[3, 4]` | `[1, 3]`, `[2, 4]` (transposed) |
| `[[1, 2]]` | `[1, 2]` in **both** cells | `[1]`, `[2]` |
| `np.array([[1, 2]])` | `1`, `2` | 0-d `array(1)`, `array(2)` stored in the cells |
| `[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]` | `[1, 2, 3]`, `[4, 5, 6]` | raises |

**Proposal:** deprecate treating a 2-D value (2-D ndarray, or a one-row DataFrame via `.iloc`) as a row under a scalar row key. After enforcement, a scalar row key means the value is 1-D over the column key and nested elements are cell values. The two layouts would then agree, the right-hand column would be fixed by construction, and the scalar-row cases that GH-64230, GH-65241 and GH-65264 had to adjudicate would go away.

Not in scope: `s.iloc[1] = np.array([5])` (length-1 array into a scalar slot), which numpy itself deprecated and pandas EAs already reject. That could be a separate deprecation.

Checked on main (3.2.0.dev0+63.gee947f39aa3).

AI disclosure: investigated and drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5.5`).

title: BUG: setitem with a 0-d ndarray key raises in iloc/loc
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

key = np.array(1)

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]}, dtype="Int64")
df.iloc[key] = 9
# TypeError: len() of unsized object
df.iloc[key, 0] = 9
# TypeError: len() of unsized object

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4.0, 5.0, 6.0]})
df.iloc[key] = 9
# TypeError: len() of unsized object

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"a": pd.date_range("2000", periods=3), "b": pd.date_range("2001", periods=3)}
)
df.iloc[key, [0, 1]] = pd.Timestamp("2010")
# ValueError: Cross index must be 1 dimensional
df.loc[key] = pd.Timestamp("2010")
# InvalidIndexError: 1
```

### Issue Description

Setting with a 0-d ndarray key raises on these paths, while the same key works for getitem (GH-21946) and for setitem on a single-dtype numpy frame or a Series.

### Expected Behavior

A 0-d ndarray key behaves like the scalar it holds, e.g. `df.iloc[np.array(1)] = 9` is the same as `df.iloc[1] = 9`. Calling `lib.item_from_zerodim` on the key (and on each entry of a tuple key) at the top of `_LocationIndexer.__setitem__` fixes all of the above, as `_getitem_axis` already does for getitem.

title: DOC: clarify and document ODS support in read_excel(), write_excel() and user guide
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

This concerns three parts of the docs:

* The [`read_excel()` docs](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.read_excel.html#pandas-read-excel)
* The [`to_excel()` docs](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.to_excel.html)
* The [IO section of the User Guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/io.html)

### Documentation problem

Even though pandas is able to read and write ODS files using `read_excel()` and `to_excel()` respectively (thanks to fixes to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/2311 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/27222), it is still difficult to find out about it. Exposing the feature further with aliases like `read_ods()` and `to_ods()` would be great in my opinion, but seeing that there is overlap between the various engines' capabilities (e.g. between calamine and odfpy) and that ODS is not the only Open Document format supported, it's not as straightforward as a plain alias with a default value for the `engine` argument. And I assume renaming the function itself to not use "Excel" would be too controversial, so this ticket is only about documentation.

Docs have been improved when fixing https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/28231 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/49790, however there are still issues:

### Suggested fix for documentation

* The [`read_excel()` docs](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.read_excel.html#pandas-read-excel) start with "Read an Excel file into a DataFrame.", which is not a full picture: "Excel file" makes it sound like it only supports file formats designed specifically to be used with Excel, so mainly `.xls` and `.xlsx`, at the exclusion of others (that are supported by Excel, or that are not tied to a specific tool). Because the actual file formats supported are already listed in the next sentence, I suggest changing the first sentence to something like: "Read Excel and Open Document formats into a DataFrame." Alternatively, it could be made more product-agnostic by using words like "spreadsheets" or "workbooks", but I think it might not be specific enough and could confuse the distinction with the `*_csv()` functions.
* The [`to_excel()` docs](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.to_excel.html) don't mention the availability of the `odf` engine. In fact, they don't mention "ODS" or "Open Document" at all. And the first sentence could be modified similarly to above.
* The [IO section of the User Guide does explain](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/io.html#opendocument-spreadsheets) how to import and export to ODS, but [its summary table](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/io.html#io-tools-text-csv-hdf5) hasn't been updated accordingly, making it look like writing to ODS is not possible.

I'm happy to submit a PR.

title: API/DEPR: what does infer_dtype of "mixed-integer" mean?
body:
We are not consistent about how we use `lib.infer_dtype(obj) == "mixed-integer"`.

- in algorithms._ensure_arraylike and infer_dtype_from_array we are using to it see if it is "safe" to call np.asarray, since we don't like numpy's behavior for e.g. `np.array(["a", 42])` which would cast `42` to `"42"`.
- in algorithms.safe_sort we're checking whether we need to use a mixed-type-friendly sorting function.
- in merge.py we're checking if dtypes are merge-compatible (i tentatively think this hides a bug)
- in strings.accesor we use it to see if we should allow the .str accessor (looks buggy)
- in arrays.boolean we use it to see if we can cast to BooleanArray (looks buggy)
- in Index._should_fallback_to_positional it determines how we treat integer keys (looks buggy)

I'm going to investigate all the buggy-looking usages here and suspect will be replacing them with more correctly-targeted checks.  But for "mixed-integer" itself, I think we should deprecate and just return "mixed"

body:
### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
The following reproduces the issue on Windows PowerShell.

First, create a copy of the website source:


Copy-Item -Recurse web\pandas "$env:TEMP\pandas-web-test"


Verify that the source files exist:


Test-Path "$env:TEMP\pandas-web-test\config.yml"
# True

Test-Path "$env:TEMP\pandas-web-test\versions.json"
# True


Then use the same directory as both `source_path` and `--target-path`:


python web\pandas_web.py "$env:TEMP\pandas-web-test" --target-path "$env:TEMP\pandas-web-test"
```

### Issue Description

The website builder deletes the source directory contents when
--target-path is the same directory as source_path.

I reproduced this using a fresh copy of web/pandas.

Before running the command, both config.yml and versions.json were
present in the source directory.

I then ran:

python web\pandas_web.py "$env:TEMP\pandas-web-test" --target-path "$env:TEMP\pandas-web-test"

The command failed with:

FileNotFoundError: ...\pandas-web-test\config.yml

After the command completed, both config.yml and versions.json were
no longer present in the source directory.

The relevant code in web/pandas_web.py is:

config_fname = source_path / "config.yml"

shutil.rmtree(target_path, ignore_errors=True)
os.makedirs(target_path, exist_ok=True)

...

context = get_context(config_fname, target_path=target_path)

When source_path and target_path refer to the same directory,
shutil.rmtree() removes the source files before config.yml is later
read.

Expected behavior:
The builder should detect that the source and target directories
overlap before deleting anything and reject the operation with a
clear error message.

I used ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Luna) to assist with investigating the code
path and drafting this issue. I reproduced and verified the behavior
myself.

### Expected Behavior

The website builder should detect that the source and target directories overlap before deleting anything.

It should reject the operation with a clear error message instead of deleting the source files.

title: BUG: DataFrame[tuple] returns a DataFrame instead of a Series for a unique full-depth key on a MultiIndex with duplicates
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
    [("col1a", "col1b"), ("col2a", "col2b"), ("col2a", "col2b")]  # duplicated (col2a, col2b)
)
df = pd.DataFrame([[10, 100, 70], [15, 120, 60]], columns=columns)

r = df[("col1a", "col1b")]   # key is unique on the MultiIndex
print(type(r))
```

### Issue Description

For a **unique full-depth tuple key**, `DataFrame.__getitem__` returns a one-column `DataFrame` instead of a `Series`, whenever the `MultiIndex` contains duplicates anywhere:

```
<class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>
  col1a
  col1b
0    10
1    15
```

Without duplicates the same code returns a `Series`:

```python
cols2 = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("a", "b"), ("c", "d"), ("e", "f")])
df2 = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], columns=cols2)
type(df2[("a", "b")])  # pandas.core.series.Series
```

The same divergence shows for `df.loc[:, full_key]` (DataFrame instead of Series), while `df.iloc[:, 0]` correctly returns a Series.

Not affected (behavior is as expected):
- A partial-depth key such as `df["col2a"]` still returns the matching sub-DataFrame.
- A duplicated full key such as `df[("col2a", "col2b")]` still returns the two matching columns.
- A single-level Index with duplicates returns a Series for a unique key — only `MultiIndex` is affected.

### Expected Behavior

A unique full-depth tuple key should select one column and return a `Series`, independent of whether other labels in the `MultiIndex` are duplicated.

### Actual Behavior

`DataFrame._getitem_multilevel` branches on `self.columns.get_loc(key)`: an int goes to the single-column Series path, a slice/ndarray goes to the sub-DataFrame path. On a non-unique `MultiIndex`, `get_loc` returns a `slice` for *every* key (even a unique full-depth one), so unique keys take the sub-DataFrame branch. This is the same underlying quirk as GH#69959 (where the unnormalized `get_loc` result broke `iloc` setitem); I found this while investigating that issue.

Downstream, the divergence breaks `df[key].tolist()`, `df[key].dtype`, and scalar broadcasting semantics for anyone reading a single column by full tuple key on a frame with duplicated MultiIndex columns.

### Installed Versions

title: BUG: groupby cumsum/cummin/cummax/rank give wrong results for datetime/timedelta columns when a group key is NaN
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "key": [0, 0, np.nan, 0],
    "td": pd.to_timedelta([1, None, 2, 3], unit="h"),
})
g = df.groupby("key")["td"]

print(g.cumsum().tolist())
# [Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00'), Timedelta('-106751992 days +20:59:05.224192'),
#  NaT, Timedelta('-106751992 days +23:59:05.224192')]

print(g.cummin().tolist())
# [Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00'), NaT, NaT, NaT]

print(g.cummax().tolist())
# [Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00'), Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00'), NaT, Timedelta('0 days 03:00:00')]

print(g.rank().tolist())
# [2.0, 1.0, nan, 3.0]

# Nanoseconds are also lost
ts = pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-01 00:00:00.000000001", "2024-01-01 00:00:00.000000002"])
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"key": [0, np.nan], "ts": ts})
print(df2.groupby("key")["ts"].cummax().iloc[0])
# 2024-01-01 00:00:00
```

### Issue Description

If a groupby key contains NaN (with the default `dropna=True`), `cumsum`, `cummin`, `cummax` and `rank` on datetime64 or timedelta64 columns return wrong results without any warning:

- `NaT` values are treated as a very large negative number instead of as missing. `cumsum` adds it to the total, `cummin` picks it, `cummax` returns the previous maximum instead of NaT, and `rank` ranks it first.
- Nanosecond precision is lost.

If the key has no NaN, the results are correct.

**Cause:** in `WrappedCythonOp._get_cython_vals` (`pandas/core/groupby/ops.py`), integer values are cast to `float64` for transforms when some keys were dropped (so that the rows with a dropped key can be filled with `NaN`):

```python
elif values.dtype.kind in "iu":
    if how in ["var", "mean"] or (
        self.kind == "transform" and self.has_dropped_na and not uses_mask
    ):
        values = ensure_float64(values)
```

Datetime and timedelta values are viewed as `int64` before this point, so they get cast as well. After the cast, `NaT` is an ordinary float, so the kernels no longer see it as missing, and values larger than 2**53 get rounded.

The same problem was fixed for nullable integer dtypes in #58811 and #65550, but not for datetime/timedelta.

**Possible fix:** don't cast datetime/timedelta values to `float64`. Instead, fill the output for the dropped rows with `NaT`.

I'd like to work on this.

### Expected Behavior

The same result as if the NaN-key rows were not there, with `NaT` (or `NaN` for `rank`) for the NaN-key rows:

```python
# cumsum
[Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00'), NaT, NaT, Timedelta('0 days 04:00:00')]
# cummin
[Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00'), NaT, NaT, Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00')]
# cummax
[Timedelta('0 days 01:00:00'), NaT, NaT, Timedelta('0 days 03:00:00')]
# rank
[1.0, nan, nan, 2.0]
# cummax (nanoseconds)
2024-01-01 00:00:00.000000001
```

title: API: warn when Timedelta/Datetime gets truncated?
body:
Context: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65608

While we now more often default to microsecond resolution, this will probably happen less often, but a remaining question raised in the above issue is whether we want to warn _if_ it happens (a bit similarly like numpy has RuntimeWarnings about division by zero or over/underflow, although we generally suppress those in pandas ..).

For example in case of:

```python
>>> ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="timedelta64[s]")
>>> ser / 2
0   0 days 00:00:00
1   0 days 00:00:01
2   0 days 00:00:01
dtype: timedelta64[s]
```

Users could get rid of the warning by either using floor division (if you are OK with loosing the fractional part) or by casting to a different unit.

title: BUG: Series.str.pad/center/ljust/rjust with a negative width raises ArrowInvalid on PyArrow-backed strings
body:
**What happened**:

`Series.str.pad`, `Series.str.center`, `Series.str.ljust` and `Series.str.rjust` raise `pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Negative buffer resize` when `width` is negative and the dtype is a PyArrow-backed string dtype.

**Reproduction** (reproduced on 3.0.6 with pyarrow 25.0.1):

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([ab, +ab, , café], dtype=pd.StringDtype(pyarrow))
s.str.ljust(-5)
# pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Negative buffer resize: -70
```

`center`, `rjust` and `pad` raise the same error. The equivalent calls on `object` dtype, `str` dtype with python storage, and Python's own `str.ljust`/`str.center` all return the strings unchanged, since a non-positive width is a no-op in Python.

**Expected behavior**:

Negative (and zero) widths should return the values unchanged, matching `object` dtype and Python string semantics.

**Root cause** (from reading the code):

`ArrowStringArrayMixin._str_pad` in `pandas/core/arrays/_arrow_string_mixins.py` passes `width` straight to `pc.utf8_lpad`/`pc.utf8_rpad`/`pc.utf8_center` for pyarrow >= 17/21. These kernels size their output buffer from `width` and raise `ArrowInvalid` for negative values. Unlike the elementwise fallback paths (which call the Python `str` methods), the kernel path has no guard.

**Notes**:

- This is pre-existing and present in released 3.0.x (unlike the `str.zfill` regression on main from #66339, tracked in #69486).
- The same family of kernels is used for `Index.str` as well.

**Installed versions**:

pandas 3.0.6, pyarrow 25.0.1, Python 3.13

title: API: Replace `na_action` with `skipna` in map methods
body:
Split out from #61128

The map methods currently take `na_action: Literal["ignore"] | None = None`:

- Series.map
- DataFrame.map
- Index.map
- CategoricalIndex.map
- ExtensionArray.map and its subclasses (Categorical, datetimelike, SparseArray, Arrow, masked)
- pandas.core.algorithms.map_array

On reading code, it seems hard to me to guess what both `na_action=None` and `na_action="ignore"` do. Better I think would be `skipna`:

```python
# current
ser.map(func, na_action=None)
ser.map(func, na_action="ignore")

# proposed
ser.map(func, skipna=False)
ser.map(func, skipna=True)         
```

Proposal

1. Add `skipna` to the methods above. The default keeps current behavior.
2. Deprecate `na_action`. Passing both na_action and skipna raises.
3. Remove `na_action` in the next major release.
4. `na_action` is positional or keyword; make `skipna` keyword-only.
5. This could have a collision with `**kwargs`. We could detect when the UDF has a `skipna` argument and act accordingly. This is of course fragile (UDFs can take `**kwargs` itself), but I think likely to catch the majority of cases, which are edgy already.

One possible concern is whether the name `skipna` is clear. For reductions, `skipna=True` means NA values are left out of the result. Here it would mean NA values are not passed to func and are kept in the output. So these are slightly different, but I personally am not too concerned by this.

title: BUG: `Series.str.zfill` with a negative width raises "Negative buffer resize" on pyarrow-backed strings (regression on main from #66339)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["1", "2", "03"], dtype="string[pyarrow]")
s.str.zfill(-2)
# pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Negative buffer resize: -20
```

### Issue Description

This is a regression on main only: the released pandas 3.0.6 returns `['1', '2', '03']` for the example above.

Since #66339, `ArrowStringArray._str_zfill` passes `width` straight to `pc.utf8_zfill` when pyarrow >= 21. For a negative
width this raises `Negative buffer resize` instead of returning the strings unchanged.

Before #66339 the same call returned `['1', '2', '03']`, which is what `str.zfill` does for any width not larger than
the string (`"1".zfill(-2) == "1"`) and what the object and python-backed string dtypes still return. The docstring
fix in #66460 also states that `Series.str.zfill` behaves identically to `str.zfill`.

A possible fix is to clamp the width (`pc.utf8_zfill(self._pa_array, max(width, 0))`) or to keep the elementwise path
for `width < 0`. cc @fangchenli 
(Found by differential testing of recent pull requests and reproduced by hand on current main.)

### Expected Behavior

```python
>>> pd.Series(["1", "2", "03"], dtype="string[pyarrow]").str.zfill(-2).tolist()
['1', '2', '03']
```

title: PERF: `df.loc[row, cols]` returns a small Series that keeps a `(len(cols), len(df))` temporary array alive (regression from 2.x)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the latest version of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import tracemalloc

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

n = 100_000
df = pd.DataFrame({c: np.zeros(n) for c in "abcd"})

res = df.loc[0, ["a", "b", "d"]]
print(getattr(res.values.base, "shape", None))  # (3, 100000)

tracemalloc.start()
results = [df.loc[0, ["a", "b", "d"]] for _ in range(100)]
print(f"{tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0] / 2**20:.0f} MiB")  # 100 Series of 3 floats
```

Output on 3.0.6 and on main (`3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e`):

```
(3, 100000)
229 MiB
```

Selecting one row and a non-contiguous list of columns returns a 3-element Series.
That Series is a view into a `(3, n)` array, which is a temporary copy made by the
column selection, not the DataFrame's own storage. Each result keeps about 2.3 MB
alive for 24 bytes of data, and the cost grows with `len(df)`. Collecting lookups
like this in a loop leads to large memory growth.

`df.iloc[0, [0, 1, 3]]` and `df[cols].loc[0]` behave the same way. Selecting the
row first (`df.loc[0][cols]`) does not.

title: BUG: .str and .dt accessors raise on dictionary-encoded ArrowDtype
body:
On current main, the `.str` and `.dt` accessors reject Series backed by dictionary-encoded `ArrowDtype`, even though the equivalent plain `ArrowDtype` (and `Categorical`, for `.str`) work fine.

Repro:

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
import datetime

# .str on dictionary-encoded strings
s = pd.Series(
    pd.array(['a', 'b', 'a'],
             dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.dictionary(pa.int32(), pa.string())))
)
s.str.upper()
# AttributeError: Can only use .str accessor with string values, not unknown-array

# .dt on dictionary-encoded timestamps
arr = pa.DictionaryArray.from_arrays(
    pa.array([0, 1, 0], type=pa.int32()),
    pa.array([datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1), datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2)],
             type=pa.timestamp('us')),
)
s2 = pd.Series(pd.arrays.ArrowExtensionArray(arr))
s2.dt.year
# AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values
```

Expected: both accessors work, decoding through the dictionary the way `Categorical` does (`pd.Series(pd.Categorical(['a', 'b', 'a'])).str.upper()` works fine).

What I found reading the code:

- `.str`: `StringMethods._validate` does `values = getattr(data, "categories", data)` to blow up categoricals before inferring. `ArrowExtensionArray` has no `.categories`, so `lib.infer_dtype` sees the raw arrow array and returns `"unknown-array"`, which is not in the allowed list.
- `.dt`: `CombinedDatetimelikeProperties.__init__` gates the arrow path on `data.dtype.kind in "Mm"`. `ArrowDtype.kind` only returns `"M"` when `pa.types.is_timestamp(self.pyarrow_dtype)` is true, which is false for dictionary types, so it falls back to the numpy object kind `"O"`.

So both accessors need to look through dictionary encoding to the value type, similar to how categoricals are handled.

Environment: pandas main (3.2.0.dev1), pyarrow 25.0.1, Python 3.12, Linux.

title: BUG: to_json(date_format="iso") segfaults on a failed allocation — NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback returns NULL without setting errorMsg
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

`int64ToIso` returns `NULL` only when its allocation fails, so the example injects a single
failed `malloc` of the exact size it requests (42 bytes for `date_unit="ms"`) with an
`LD_PRELOAD` shim. Nothing else about the frame is unusual.

```c
// failmalloc.c — gcc -shared -fPIC -o failmalloc.so failmalloc.c -ldl
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <dlfcn.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static size_t target_size = 0;
static int armed = 0, fired = 0;

void failmalloc_arm(size_t size) { target_size = size; armed = 1; fired = 0; }

void *malloc(size_t size) {
  static void *(*real)(size_t) = NULL;
  if (!real)
    real = dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "malloc");
  if (armed && !fired && size == target_size) {
    fired = 1;
    fprintf(stderr, "[failmalloc] returning NULL for size=%zu\n", size);
    return NULL;
  }
  return real(size);
}
```

```python
# repro.py
import ctypes, faulthandler
import pandas as pd

faulthandler.enable()

frame = pd.DataFrame({"t": pd.to_datetime([1616409000123] * 50, unit="ms").as_unit("ms")})

ctypes.CDLL("./failmalloc.so").failmalloc_arm(ctypes.c_size_t(42))

print(frame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso"))
```

```
$ PYTHONMALLOC=malloc LD_PRELOAD=./failmalloc.so python repro.py
[failmalloc] returning NULL for size=42
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x0000004002102f00 [python] (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 292 in write
  File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 241 in to_json
  File ".../pandas/core/generic.py", line 2623 in to_json
  File "repro.py", line 12 in <module>

Current thread's C stack trace (most recent call first):
  ...
  Binary file ".../pandas/_libs/json.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so", at +0x8ae0
```

### Issue Description

A failed allocation inside the ISO datetime conversion is dereferenced as a `NULL` string
instead of raising, because the encoder's `NULL` signal is `enc->errorMsg` and this path never
sets it:

1. `int64ToIso` (`pandas/_libs/src/datetime/date_conversions.c`) allocates the output buffer and
   returns `NULL` after `PyErr_NoMemory()` if that fails. It also returns `NULL` when
   `make_iso_8601_datetime` fails.
2. `NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback` (`pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c`) forwards
   that result unchanged, without setting `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg`.
3. `ultrajsonenc.c`, `case JT_UTF8`, tests only `enc->errorMsg` before using the value:

```c
    value = enc->getStringValue(obj, &tc, &szlen);
    if (enc->errorMsg) {
      enc->endTypeContext(obj, &tc);
      return;
    }
    Buffer_Reserve(enc, RESERVE_STRING(szlen));
    ...
      if (!Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated(enc, value, value + szlen)) {
```

So `Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated` runs on `value == NULL`, which segfaults.

Sibling callbacks in the same file follow the opposite convention and do set `errorMsg` before
returning `NULL` — `PyTimeToJSON` and the type-check branch of `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` both
do `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg = "";`. Two more callbacks look to have the
same gap as the one above:

- `NpyTimeDeltaToIsoCallback` forwards `int64ToIsoDuration`, which has the same two `NULL`
  returns.
- `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` sets `errorMsg` for the type check, but forwards the result of
  `PyDateTimeToIso` (which has several `NULL` returns) unchecked.

This looks like a remaining instance of the class of bug reported in #66356 and fixed by #66357
and #66797 — neither of those passes touched the ISO datetime/timedelta callbacks.

Reproduced on 3.0.5 and on `main` at `3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e`, both Python 3.14 /
linux-x86_64. 3.0.6 contains no changes to these files.

For context on why this isn't only theoretical: we hit a SIGSEGV in `pandas/_libs/json...so`
beneath `DataFrame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso")` in CI, serialising a ~45k-row
frame with a tz-aware `datetime64[ms, UTC]` column under memory pressure from several parallel
test workers. I can't attribute that crash with certainty — the shipped extension module is
stripped, so the C stack has no symbols — but this is the only unchecked-`NULL` path I could
find on it, and the per-value allocation count makes a transient failure plausible.

### Expected Behavior

`MemoryError` (or the relevant exception) propagates to the caller, consistent with how other
allocation failures in the encoder are handled — e.g. `Buffer_Realloc` calls
`SetError(NULL, enc, "Could not reserve memory block")`.

Setting `errorMsg` in the three callbacks before returning `NULL` would be enough; adding a
`value == NULL` check alongside the `enc->errorMsg` check in `JT_UTF8` would make the encoder
robust to any future callback with the same omission.

title: ENH: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Long-running Series.apply() and DataFrame.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination.

Currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. If the Python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed.

It would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution.

For example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. If execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows.

This could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations such as API requests, machine learning inference, LLM calls, network operations, or computationally expensive transformations.

The goal would not be to handle the process crash itself, since pandas cannot execute recovery code after the process has already terminated. Instead, intermediate results would be persisted proactively during normal execution so that they can be recovered afterwards.

### Feature Description

result = df[“column”].apply(
expensive_function,
checkpoint=“apply_checkpoint.pkl”,
checkpoint_every=10,
)

### Alternative Solutions

for i, value in df["column"].items():
    df.at[i, "result"] = expensive_function(value)

    if i % 10 == 0:
        df.to_pickle("checkpoint.pkl")

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: BUG: loc assignment of a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow column raises TypeError
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df.loc[:, "A"] = df["A"].astype(float).round(6)
# TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]'

df2 = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0, 5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df2.loc[:, "A"] = df2["A"].astype(float).round(6)  # OK
```

### Issue Description

On a 1-row DataFrame, df.loc[:, col] = <NumPy ndarray/Series> into an existing PyArrow-backed column raises TypeError, even when every value is a valid float (e.g. 5000.0). The same assignment succeeds when the frame has 2 or more rows.

5000.0 is not invalid. The error text is misleading.

What happens:

The RHS is a length-1 float64 array, array([5000.]).
SingleBlockManager.setitem_inplace unwraps any 1-d length-1 ndarray to a 0-d array to avoid the NumPy 1.25 deprecation (value[0, ...], added in [#52906](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/52906)):
if isinstance(value, np.ndarray) and value.ndim == 1 and len(value) == 1:
    value = value[0, ...]  # array([5000.]) -> array(5000.)
is_list_like(array(5000.)) is False, so ArrowExtensionArray._box_pa takes the scalar path.
pa.scalar(np.ndarray(...), type=pa.float64()) fails:
ArrowInvalid: Could not convert array(5000.) with type numpy.ndarray: tried to convert to double
pandas 3 rewraps that as TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]' and, unlike 2.x, does not fall back to recasting the column.
This is the same unwrap that #59249 / #57923 / #65452 discuss for object-dtype cells. Here the symptom is different and is a hard error on valid numeric data, not an API question about whether a cell should store array([1.]) vs 1.0.

Related, but not the same report:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/59249
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/57923
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65452

### Expected Behavior

A valid float should be written into the double[pyarrow] column. 1-row and N-row frames should behave the same.

A narrow fix would be enough and does not require settling the whole single-element listlike-RHS matrix in #65452, for example:

in _box_pa_scalar, if value is a 0-d ndarray, use value.item() before pa.scalar, or
in setitem_inplace, skip the length-1 unwrap when the target is an ExtensionArray.

### Installed Versions

<details>

python   : 3.13.5
pandas   : 3.0.5   (also reproduced the failure mode on 3.0.6 source; main still has the unwrap)
pyarrow  : 25.0.0
numpy    : 2.5.2
OS       : Windows

On pandas 2.2.3 / 2.3.3 the same assignment does not raise. It emits

FutureWarning: Setting an item of incompatible dtype is deprecated...

and recasts the column to NumPy float64. pandas 3 turned that warning into this TypeError, so the 1-row unwrap now surfaces as a hard failure on Arrow columns.

Confirmed on all released pandas 3.0.x; 3.0.6 fixed a different loc[:, col] Arrow issue (GH 67990, CoW aliasing), not this one.

</details>

title: ENH: ArrowExtensionArray should be supported by HDFStore
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Currently, writing data containing ArrowExtensionArrays to HDF5 fails. Since Numpy objects are pickled anyways, I don't see why Pandas should not also automatically pickle ArrowExtensionArrays.

For NumPy pickling, see these lines: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4fde542d9691acc218c6293165619dcb397e6a8b/pandas/io/pytables.py#L3998-L4001

For a minimal working example (not working) - to test with both pa.array examples:

```
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

# Nested Arrow array
#arr = pa.array([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5, 6]])
arr = pa.array([["123"]])

# DataFrame with Arrow-backed column
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "jets": pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type))
    }
)

# Triggers PyTables serialization
df.to_hdf("test.h5", key="df")
```

### Feature Description

The cheapest solution is to add

```python3
            elif isinstance(value.dtype, ArrowDtype):
                vlarr = self._handle.create_vlarray(
                    self.group, key, _tables().ObjectAtom(), filters=self._filters
                )
                vlarr.append(value)
```

below the branch https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4fde542d9691acc218c6293165619dcb397e6a8b/pandas/io/pytables.py#L4024 .

### Alternative Solutions

One could also check array types and e.g. string arrays could be saved correctly. However then after loading, they are no longer PyArrow data and this does not solve saving arbitrary data.

### Additional Context

Since Uproot uses ExtensionArrays in https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/pull/734 , Uproot loaded data can no longer always be stored as HDF5. This is described in https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/issues/1706 .
It is realistic that Uproot moves to ArrowExtensionArrays - at least I suggested that in Pull Request https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/pull/1718 . Currently it uses `AwkwardExtensionArray` from `awkward-pandas`, but that is deprecated.
Meaning the effort of not fearing failures when saving data read from a ROOT file as HDF5 now transferred to making Pandas support `ArrowExtensionArray`s for HDF5 export.

title: API: should the _supports_2d contract require repeat(axis=...)?
body:
`ExtensionDtype._supports_2d` documents what a third-party array must provide to
declare itself 2-D capable (`pandas/core/dtypes/base.py`):

> Arrays that support 2D values should:
>
> - implement Array.reshape
> - subclass the Dim2CompatTests in tests.extension.base
> - `_concat_same_type` should support `axis` keyword
> - `_reduce` and reductions should support `axis` keyword

`repeat` is not on that list, and the base implementation actively rejects an axis:

```python
# pandas/core/arrays/base.py
def repeat(self, repeats, axis: AxisInt | None = None) -> Self:
    nv.validate_repeat((), {"axis": axis})
```

while the backing-array implementation both defaults to and honours one:

```python
# pandas/_libs/arrays.pyx
def repeat(self, repeats, axis: int | np.integer = 0):
```

In-tree this never shows, because the only dtypes with `_supports_2d = True` are
`DatetimeTZDtype` and `PeriodDtype`, whose arrays are `NDArrayBacked`. A third-party
array that implements the four documented requirements and inherits
`ExtensionArray.repeat` would raise
`ValueError: the 'axis' parameter is not supported in the pandas implementation of repeat()`.

This matters because the gate internals use to decide "may I treat this as 2-D" is

```python
def is_1d_only_ea_dtype(dtype) -> bool:
    return isinstance(dtype, ExtensionDtype) and not dtype._supports_2d
```

so anything reaching a 2-D code path is exactly the `_supports_2d` audience. Broadcasting
a 1-D value across several columns wants `value.reshape(1, -1).repeat(ncols, axis=0)`, which
works for both in-tree types and for any `NDArrayBacked` array, but is not something the
documented contract entitles pandas to call.

Two ways to resolve it:

1. Add `repeat` with `axis` support to the `_supports_2d` requirements, and relax the base
   signature/validation for 2-D-capable arrays. This documents what pandas already needs and
   costs existing third-party authors nothing until they opt into `_supports_2d`.
2. Treat `repeat(axis=)` as out of contract and require internals to spell 2-D broadcasting
   with only the four documented operations, e.g. `value.repeat(ncols).reshape(-1, ncols)`.
   That is contract-clean but produces a C-contiguous result where the current spelling gives
   an F-contiguous one, which changes the stored block's layout on the NumPy path.

No in-tree caller passes `axis=` to an ExtensionArray's `repeat` today, so nothing is broken
right now; this is about whether such a call is legitimate going forward.

title: BUG: Value-dependent formatting when casting from datetime to string
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

assert pd.__version__ == "3.0.5"
assert np.__version__ == "2.5.1"

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:01"],  # <- value dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:01.000"],  # <- unit dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
```

### Issue Description

The string formatting of datetimes depends on the values rather than the time unit of the data type. The analogous operation in NumPy only depends on the unit.

I was not able to find a definitive answer on the matter that clarified whether this is intended behavior. I can see that this may have been intended in pandas 1.x where the one and only unit was `ns` which would lead to very long strings in all cases, despite most users probably never working on a ns resolution. 

### Expected Behavior

My understanding is that value-dependent semantics are not desired in pandas these days(?). Given that pandas allows users to define their desired units these days, it seems reasonable to me to make the formatting depend only on the unit rather than the values. 

Alternatively, it may be nice to document the intended formatting semantics (unless I missed them and that is already the case).

title: BUG/DEPR: low_memory keyword in read_csv
body:
`low_memory=True` (the default) can give incorrect results in corner cases, which is the reason why the keyword exists.  Minimal example:

```
N = 65536  # rows in the first internal chunk of an 8-column table
data = (
    "a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h\n"
    + "1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n" * N          # chunk 1 -> int64
    + f"{2**64 - 1},1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n"   # chunk 2 -> uint64
    + f"{2**64 - 2},1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n"
)

res = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data))["a"]
exp = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), low_memory=False)["a"]

assert exp.iloc[-1] != exp.iloc[-2]
assert res.iloc[-1] != res.iloc[-2]  #  <- fails because of unwanted casting
```

In the `low_memory=True` case, we do dtype inference in chunks.  In cases where different chunks get different dtypes, the concat does a cast which can be lossy.  `low_memory=False` avoids that by doing the dtype inference on the whole column instead of in chunks.

The alternative I think we should consider is to detect when this casting occurs and then re-parse (with `usecols` restricted to the affected column) in the `low_memory=False` mode.  Then we get the correct result and don't need the user-facing keyword.  The downside is a perf penalty in these corner cases.

Passing `low_memory=False` disables the parallel path, which is what brought this to my attention.

title: DEPR: cache_dates in read_csv
body:
A review of github code shows that cache_dates is the least-used keyword, with 8.4k uses (compared to 1.01M of dtype).  Moreover, the cases where `cache_dates=False` improves performance are fewer and fewer now that ISO cases get excluded by default.

I think we should deprecate the keyword and have a slightly simpler API.  cc @mroeschke

title: API: select_dtypes
body:
We made a bunch of changes to select_dtypes in July.  I advocate reverting the most niche use cases to simplify the code.  

Summarizing the support that was *added*:

1) Passing an ExtensionDtype class matches every instance of that dtype (instead of raising)
2) Passing a partially-specified IntervalDtype e.g. IntervalDtype(np.int64) (without specifying "closed") matches all IntervalDtypes that match that partial specification.
3) Passing a partially-specified CategoricalDtype e.g. CategoricalDtype(my_categories, ordered=None) matches all CategoricalDtypes with those categories regardless of orderedness.

Summarizing the behavior that *changed* as bugfixes

4) Passing a specific dtype e.g. `np.dtype(np.int64)` matches exactly that dtype, not every integer dtype.
5) Passing a type (that isn't an ExtesnsionDtype subclass) raises instead of matching object dtype.
6) Passing EADtypes like Int64Dtype() would match numpy integer dtypes.

Summarizing deprecations

7) Deprecated accepting "datetimetz" and "datetime64tz" since item 1 now means you can pass pd.DatetimeTZDtype explicitly.

I advocate reverting items 2 and 3 before 3.1 is released, as they contribute a lot of complexity for very niche use cases.  Also we don't have a mechanism to do similar partial-specification matching for DatetimeTZDtype or 3rd party EAs.

I couldn't open a bug report because the form requires confirmation that the bug exists in the latest stable release. This parallel path is only on main and is not included in pandas 3.0.5, so I couldn't truthfully check that box. I'm reporting it here instead.

I found an issue in the parallel read_csv path when using converters=. On the official 3.1.0.dev0+1870.g27449ca07b nightly, a stateful converter produced different results with mode.max_threads=4 and mode.max_threads=1.

title: ENH: move the postgresql extra from psycopg2 to psycopg 3
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

`pip install pandas[postgresql]` still installs psycopg2. Current pin on
main, in `[project.optional-dependencies]`:

    postgresql = ['SQLAlchemy>=2.0.42', 'psycopg2>=2.9.10', 'adbc-driver-postgresql>=1.7.0']

After #67968 the SQL user guide names psycopg 3 as the example SQLAlchemy
driver for PostgreSQL, so the packaging and the docs now point at different
generations of the driver. This came up in the review of that PR:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/67968#discussion_r3984002256

I wish `pandas[postgresql]` installed the driver the docs recommend.

### Feature Description

Swap `psycopg2>=2.9.10` for a `psycopg` (3.x) pin with an appropriate
floor, moving the coupled spots together:

- the `postgresql` extra in `pyproject.toml`
- the `all` extra in `pyproject.toml` (same psycopg2 pin today)
- `environment.yml`
- the optional-dependencies table in `doc/source/getting_started/install.rst`
  (lists psycopg2 as the PostgreSQL engine for SQLAlchemy)

The psycopg project describes psycopg2 as fully supported for legacy
applications and recommends psycopg 3 for new projects. One compatibility
question decides the floor and the shape of the change: in SQLAlchemy,
psycopg2 remains the default dialect for bare `postgresql://` URLs, so
replacing the pin changes what a fresh `pandas[postgresql]` install can
connect with unless the engine string is explicit.

### Alternative Solutions

- Ship both drivers in the extra (`psycopg` and `psycopg2`): no breakage
  for users relying on psycopg2 being pulled in, at the cost of a heavier
  install. The two packages coexist and SQLAlchemy picks the dialect from
  the URL scheme.
- Keep psycopg2 and treat the docs recommendation and the extra as
  separate concerns; the user guide already shows both dialect strings
  explicitly.
- Replace psycopg2 with psycopg and accept that bare `postgresql://`
  users must add psycopg2 themselves or move to the explicit
  `postgresql+psycopg` scheme shown in the user guide.

### Additional Context

- Raised by @jbrockmendel  in the review of #67968 (link above).
- psycopg project statement: "Psycopg 2 remains fully supported for legacy
  applications. New projects should use Psycopg 3." (psycopg.org)
- SQLAlchemy 2.0 dialect docs: psycopg2 "remains the default dialect for
  the `postgresql://` dialect series"; psycopg 3 requires the explicit
  `postgresql+psycopg` scheme.
- I run the explicit `postgresql+psycopg` path in production (pipeline
  loading ~46M rows per day into PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB, psycopg 3.3.4
  with SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 against PostgreSQL 17).

title: BUG: mixed int64/float64 Index operations falsely match distinct labels above 2**53
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

integer_label = 2**53 + 1                  # 9007199254740993
float_label = float(2**53)                 # 9007199254740992.0

integer_index = pd.Index([integer_label], dtype="int64")
float_index = pd.Index([float_label], dtype="float64")

print(integer_label == float_label)
print("equals:", integer_index.equals(float_index))

try:
    integer_index.get_loc(float_label)
except KeyError:
    print("get_loc: KeyError")

print("get_indexer:", integer_index.get_indexer(float_index))
print("intersection:", integer_index.intersection(float_index))
print("union:", integer_index.union(float_index))
print("difference:", integer_index.difference(float_index))

values = pd.Series(["payload"], index=integer_index)
print("reindex:")
print(values.reindex(float_index))

left = pd.Series([1], index=integer_index)
right = pd.Series([2], index=float_index)
print("aligned addition:")
print(left + right)


Output on pandas 3.0.5:


False
equals: True
get_loc: KeyError
get_indexer: [0]
intersection: Index([9007199254740993], dtype='int64')
union: Index([9007199254740992.0], dtype='float64')
difference: Index([], dtype='int64')
reindex:
9.007199e+15    payload
dtype: str
aligned addition:
9007199254740993    3
dtype: int64
```

### Issue Description

The two labels are distinct: Python equality returns `False`, and scalar `Index.get_loc` raises `KeyError`. However, `get_indexer` returns `[0]`. False matches also occur in Index set operations, reindexing, and arithmetic alignment.

This is not a case where the original integer has already been lost inside a float. The float label is exactly `2**53`, while the integer label is exactly `2**53 + 1`. They become equal only after the integer Index is cast to `float64` during mixed-dtype reconciliation.

Source inspection identifies more than one relevant path. For mismatched `int64`/`float64` dtypes, `get_indexer` calls `_find_common_type_compat`, casts both operands to `float64`, and then calls `_get_indexer`. This conversion rounds `2**53 + 1` to `2**53`.

Separately, `Index.equals` compares the underlying arrays through `array_equivalent` and returns `True` for these two Index objects. Both `intersection` and `difference` have early-return paths based on `Index.equals`, before their general matching logic. The observed results should therefore not all be attributed solely to `get_indexer`.

The practical consequence is silent association of data with a different label. Large numeric identifiers, transaction numbers, or similar keys can reach this path when one source uses `int64` and another uses `float64`, for example after an import or missing-value-driven conversion.

Related but distinct: #61676 and #66794 concern false matches in `isin`. That path now returns `False` for this pair on current main, while `get_indexer`, set operations, reindexing, and alignment still produce the results above. Merge dtype/precision reports such as #8596 and #61688 concern different APIs.

I found no identical public Issue or PR in searches for the concrete value `9007199254740993`, `2**53`, mixed `int64`/`float64` Index operations, and `get_indexer`. This does not guarantee that no duplicate exists.

### Automated tools disclosure

I used OpenAI Codex (GPT-5; reasoning-effort setting not exposed) for English translation and formatting of this report. I reviewed the final issue text before submission.

### Expected Behavior

Mixed numeric Index operations should not match labels that are unequal before dtype reconciliation. For the example above:

```text
integer_index.get_indexer(float_index) -> array([-1])
integer_index.intersection(float_index) -> empty Index
integer_index.union(float_index) -> two distinct labels
integer_index.difference(float_index) -> the original integer label
values.reindex(float_index) -> missing value, not "payload"
left + right -> two distinct labels with missing values
```

The exact result dtype for operations that must contain both labels may require a compatibility decision, but both exact values must be preserved as distinct labels.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

values = [0.0, np.nan]
dense = pd.Series(values)
sparse = pd.Series(pd.arrays.SparseArray(values, fill_value=0.0))
frame = sparse.to_frame("a")

print(sparse.any())
print(sparse.any(skipna=True))
print(dense.any(skipna=True))

print(sparse.any(skipna=False))
print(dense.any(skipna=False))

print(frame.any(skipna=True)["a"])
print(frame.any(skipna=False)["a"])


Output:


True
True
False
False
True
True
False
```

### Issue Description

For `float64` data containing `np.nan`, `Series.any` gives the opposite `skipna` behavior when the Series is backed by a `SparseArray`. `DataFrame.any` shows the same behavior for a single `SparseArray`-backed column with the default `axis=0`. With `skipna=True`, the missing value is retained and makes the result `True`. With `skipna=False`, the missing value is dropped and the result becomes `False`.

This is a silent result difference from an equivalent dense Series. It also affects the default call, because `Series.any()` defaults to `skipna=True`.

The behavior appears to come from the non-skipna-aware branch of `SparseArray._reduce`, which currently selects the original array when `skipna=True` and calls `dropna()` when `skipna=False`:

```python
if skipna:
    arr = self
else:
    arr = self.dropna()
```

Related but distinct work: #65478 concerns `SparseArray.mean` accepting `skipna`, and #68194 adds other SparseArray reductions. Neither appears to cover the reversed `Series.any` results above.

The reversed preprocessing branch appears to date back to commit
`56d8e789155231b04131c6bf4674971ec3f38f95` (#22325, October 13, 2018),
which made `SparseArray` an `ExtensionArray` and added `SparseArray._reduce`.
It is present in the v0.24.0 source and in every sampled release line through
3.0.5, as well as current main. The first release containing it appears to be
pandas 0.24.0.

### Automated tools disclosure

I used OpenAI Codex (GPT-5; reasoning-effort setting not exposed) for English
translation and formatting of this report. I reviewed the final issue text
before submission.

### Expected Behavior

The sparse and dense Series should return the same results:

```text
sparse.any()             -> False
sparse.any(skipna=True)  -> False
sparse.any(skipna=False) -> True
frame.any(skipna=True)   -> False
frame.any(skipna=False)  -> True
```

Equivalently, the non-skipna-aware preprocessing should drop missing values when `skipna=True`, not when it is `False`.

title: BUG: IntervalIndex set ops and astype/constructor raise TypeError when passed a RangeIndex
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

iv = pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks([0, 2, 4])

iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(0))
# TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)

iv.symmetric_difference(pd.RangeIndex(0))
# TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)

pd.RangeIndex(0).union(iv)
# TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)

pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(0))
# TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)

pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(2, 4))
# TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)
```

### Issue Description

The same operations succeed with any other empty array-like, e.g.:

```python
iv.union(pd.Index([], dtype="int64"))   # IntervalIndex([(0, 2], (2, 4]], dtype='interval[int64, right]')
iv.union(np.array([], dtype=np.int64))  # OK
iv.union(pd.Series([], dtype="int64"))  # OK
iv.union([])                            # OK
```

A non-empty ``RangeIndex`` with incompatible dtype also works (falls back to object dtype):
``iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(2, 4))`` -> ``Index([(0, 2], (2, 4], 2, 3], dtype='object')``.

Only ``RangeIndex`` arguments crash, both empty and non-empty (in the direct constructor), on both the LHS and RHS of set operations.

**Root cause** (observed on main, ``cb13b0e9a4``): in ``pandas/core/arrays/interval.py``, ``_maybe_convert_platform_interval`` only converts ``values`` to an ndarray when it lacks a ``dtype`` attribute:

```python
if not hasattr(values, "dtype"):
    values = np.asarray(values)
```

``RangeIndex`` has a ``dtype``, so it is passed through unchanged to the Cython function ``intervals_to_interval_bounds``, which requires an ndarray and raises ``TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)``.

Trigger paths:
1. Direct: ``pd.IntervalIndex(RangeIndex(...))`` / ``IntervalArray(RangeIndex(...))`` / ``RangeIndex.astype("interval")``.
2. Set ops: ``IntervalIndex.union`` with an empty ``other`` where ``_find_common_type_compat(other)`` resolves to ``interval[int64, right]`` (empty ``RangeIndex``; an empty ``Index`` instead resolves to ``object``), then ``other.astype(interval_dtype)`` raises before the empty-``other`` short-circuit is reached.

### Expected Behavior

Set operations between an ``IntervalIndex`` and an empty ``RangeIndex`` should behave like the other empty array-likes (union/symmetric_difference return the original interval index), and constructing an ``IntervalIndex`` from a ``RangeIndex`` should either work consistently or raise the regular ``TypeError: ... is not an interval`` message (matching ``pd.IntervalIndex([2, 3])``), not a Cython ``TypeError`` about internal argument types.

A fix converting ``RangeIndex`` to an ndarray in ``_maybe_convert_platform_interval`` (as is already done for empty lists, ``GH19016``) resolves all of the cases above.
