title: BUG: parallel read_csv (GH-64347) diverges from the serial path in several cases
body:
Adversarial testing of the parallel `read_csv` path added in GH-64347 turned up several cases where the parallel result diverges from the serial (`mode.max_threads=1`) result on the *same* file. Reporting them together since most share a root cause. All reproduce on `main` through the default path on a non-Windows machine (files must exceed the 50 MB parallel threshold).

### Root cause for most of these: the parallel path ignores `low_memory=False`

`_can_parallelize_csv` never consults `low_memory`, so `read_csv(big_file, low_memory=False)` is still split into `n_workers` byte-range chunks. That reintroduces exactly the per-chunk type/NA-inference divergences that `low_memory=False` exists to prevent: a "lean" chunk sees a different value distribution than the whole file and infers differently. Bug 2 and Bug 3 below are both instances of this.

---

### 🔴 Bug 1 — `EmptyDataError` on a valid headerless file with a blank first line

`header=None` (without `names`) on a file whose first physical line is blank or whitespace-only raises, where the serial path reads it fine (it skips the blank line).

```python
import os, pandas as pd

with open("f1.csv", "wb") as fh:
    fh.write(b"\n")  # leading blank line
    fh.write(b"".join(f"{i},{i*2},x{i}\n".encode() for i in range(2_600_000)))  # ~59 MB

pd.read_csv("f1.csv", header=None)
# -> EmptyDataError: No columns to parse from file

with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    pd.read_csv("f1.csv", header=None)   # OK, (2600000, 3)
```

**Cause:** in `_read_csv_parallel`, column-name inference builds `name_buf = preamble + first_line`; when `first_line` is blank, `TextFileReader(name_buf, ...)` raises `EmptyDataError`. That is not a `ParserError` subclass, so the `except (ParserError, UnicodeDecodeError)` fallback in `_read` doesn't catch it. Also fires when `skiprows` lands `data_start` on a blank line with `header=None`. (The `names=[...]` form falls back cleanly via the `n_first_rows != 1` guard — only bare `header=None` crashes.)

**Fix:** catch `EmptyDataError` around the name-inference `TextFileReader` and `return None` (fall back). Falling back is always safe: if the serial path would also raise, we reproduce it. Validated locally, 78 tests in `test_parallel_read.py` still pass.

---

### 🔴 Bug 2 — `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` raises on large ints where serial succeeds

A chunk that sees only large integers (> 2⁵³) attempts a numeric/pyarrow conversion and raises, while the whole-file serial read keeps the column as `double`/string.

```python
import pandas as pd

BIG = "9223372036854775807"
with open("f2.csv", "w") as fh:
    fh.write("c0\n")
    fh.write("\n".join("1.5" if i == 2_000_000 else BIG for i in range(4_000_000)))  # ~76 MB
    fh.write("\n")

pd.read_csv("f2.csv", dtype_backend="pyarrow", low_memory=False)
# -> pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Integer value 9223372036854775807 not in range ...

with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    pd.read_csv("f2.csv", dtype_backend="pyarrow", low_memory=False)   # OK, dtype double[pyarrow]
```

The guard treats `int`-kind + `float`-kind chunks as safe to `concat`, which holds for numpy/`numpy_nullable` but not pyarrow (its `concat` does a checked int→double cast that fails above 2⁵³). Depending on magnitude the parallel path raises `ArrowInvalid` (int in `[2⁵³, 2⁶⁴)`) or `OverflowError` (`> 2⁶⁴`). This is **pyarrow-specific** — `numpy` and `numpy_nullable` match serial in all cases tested. Note that with the default `low_memory=True`, a large file makes the serial path chunk internally too, so *both* raise; the clean parallel-only regression is under `low_memory=False`.

---

### 🔴 Bug 3 — Silent NA-mask divergence (wrong data, no error)

This is the most concerning: no exception, wrong values. NA tokens are kept as literal strings instead of NA when a chunk contains only `{NA-token} + {int in [2⁶³, 2⁶⁴-1]}`.

```python
import pandas as pd

OVER = "9223372036854775808"  # 2**63
with open("f3.csv", "w") as fh:
    fh.write("c0\nabc\n")
    fh.write("\n".join("nan" if i % 5 == 0 else OVER for i in range(4_000_000)))  # ~64 MB
    fh.write("\n")

par = pd.read_csv("f3.csv", low_memory=False)
with pd.option_context("mode.max_threads", 1):
    ser = pd.read_csv("f3.csv", low_memory=False)

ser["c0"].isna().sum()   # 800000  (all "nan" -> NA)
par["c0"].isna().sum()   # 200000  (600000 "nan" kept as the literal string "nan")
```

Both columns have dtype `str`, so the per-column dtype reconciliation (`_read_csv_parallel`, which compares only `dtype.kind`) sees `str == str` and concatenates without falling back.

**Mechanism.** A chunk of only `{NA-token, uint64-range int}` overflows int64 → retries uint64 → hits `uint64_conflict` (`seen_uint && seen_null`) → routed to the "leave AS IS" branch in `_convert_tokens`, which calls `_string_convert(..., na_filter=0, ...)` (`parsers.pyx` ~L1139 / ~L1147) and emits NA tokens literally. The whole-file serial read also contains `abc`, so it takes the object branch with the real `na_filter` and masks NA. This affects default NA tokens **and** custom `na_values` (list and dict), under object/`str`/pyarrow/`numpy_nullable`. It does **not** affect empty strings, bool+NA, values that overflow uint64, or `keep_default_na=False`.

**Note on the fix:** the `na_filter=0` "AS IS" emission is intentional and tested (`test_na_values_uint64`, GH-14983 asserts uint64-conflict columns are kept literal), so this can't be fixed by simply passing `na_filter` through — that reverts GH-14983. The parallel-specific regression should instead be addressed by respecting `low_memory=False` (see below). The default `low_memory=True` case can't be made byte-identical to a whole-file read without giving up parallelism, since serial `low_memory` already gives context-dependent NA here — probably a doc note.

---

### Lower-severity

- **Bug 4 — inconsistent error *type* for incompatible explicit `dtype`.** `dtype={"c": "Int64"}` on a column of mixed float/overflow-int can raise `OverflowError` from the parallel path vs `TypeError` from serial. Both fail; only the message differs. It is deterministic (the first chunk's error propagates via ordered `future.result()`), not a thread race.
- **Bug 5 — duplicated warnings from worker threads.** A converter+dtype `ParserWarning` fires once per chunk from the `ThreadPoolExecutor` workers (serial: 1, parallel: N), with a racy `stacklevel`.
- **Bug 6 — mmap unmap deferred on the error path.** When a worker raises anything other than `ParserError`/`UnicodeDecodeError`, its traceback pins the memoryview, so `mm.close()` raises `BufferError` and is suppressed; the mapping is unmapped only when the traceback is GC'd (transient address-space/FD hold). Bug 1 and Bug 2 both exercise this path.

---

### Suggested fixes

1. **Bug 1** — catch `EmptyDataError` in name inference → `return None`.
2. **`low_memory=False` gate** — `if kwds.get("low_memory") is False: return False` in `_can_parallelize_csv`. This removes the parallel-specific part of both **Bug 2** and **Bug 3** for callers who opted out of chunked inference. (Validated: they fall back and match, 78 tests pass.)
3. **Bug 2** under default `low_memory` — additionally gate `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` or fall back when a pyarrow int chunk exceeds 2⁵³.
4. **Bug 5 / Bug 6** — polish; Bug 6 is roughly a one-liner.

### Verified solid (no divergence found)

Thread/memory safety under a 250×-repeat concurrency stress (byte-identical every run; the SIMD tokenizer scan never over-reads past the mmap end); quoted embedded newlines (a boundary inside a quote always leaves a chunk mid-quote → `EOF inside string` → fallback, incl. a 50k-embedded-newline field spanning 16 chunks); the byte-offset/chunk-boundary math (1-row × 16-worker, multibyte headers, giant lines, huge preambles); `dtype="category"`, `encoding_errors`, BOM/CRLF/no-trailing-newline, thousands/decimal, uint64+NA precision, and wide/multi-column reads.

Not tested here (would need a different environment): free-threaded (no-GIL) builds, Windows/Linux specifics.

title: BUG:  `cummax` / `cummin` incorrect for pyarrow floating dtypes
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([-4.0, -3.0, -2.0, -1.0], dtype="float64[pyarrow]")
print(s.cummax())
```

### Issue Description

`Series.cummax()` / `DataFrame.cummax()` on a pyarrow floating dtype ( `float32[pyarrow]` / `float64[pyarrow]` ) silently returns a tiny sentinel (~2.2e-308, which prints as 0.0) instead of the true running maximum whenever the running max is negative (or zero/subnormal), because the underlying `pyarrow.compute.cumulative_max` call omits start, so pyarrow defaults it to the smallest positive float instead of `-inf`. The same root cause makes `cummin` return a wrong value when the running min is `+inf` 

### Expected Behavior

`cummax` should return the true running maximum (e.g. [-4, -3, -2, -1] for [-4, -3, -2, -1]), matching the numpy-backed dtype, instead of 0.0.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

x1 = pd.DataFrame([1, 2, 3, 4, np.nan, None], columns=["col"], dtype="float64")
select = x1.columns == "not_in_columns"
print("is slice empty:", x1.loc[:, select].empty)

x2 = pd.DataFrame([1, 2, 3, 4, np.nan, None], columns=["col"], dtype="Float64")

x2.loc[:, select] = pd.NA  # same with np.nan
print(x2)
```

### Issue Description

New Float64 vs old float64 (note capitalization) yields different results, when sliced by empty dataframe. In the attached sample code, in both cases we slice with empty df, however the NAN assignment goes through for Float64 dtype. The float64 behaves as expected and the assignment is ignored. 

The correct behaviour of the "float64":

select = x1.columns == "not_in_columns"

0  1.0

2  3.0

title: CI: Unpin CI dependencies
body:
With the release of `pytest` 9.1.1, the `pytest<9.1` pin in [`unit-tests.yml`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/ead0d998c4672966991c0380ba7a65e522c16355/.github/workflows/unit-tests.yml) is no longer needed.

Additionally, the `meson` pin prevents us from using new Meson features, such as the NumPy dependency (xref #63703). AFAIU, it was pinned to prevent warnings from failing builds under `-Werror`. It's possible to unpin it and handle any resulting warnings using specific `-Wno-...` flags instead.

title: Consider adding a changelog to track version history
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
A `CHANGELOG.md` file would help users understand what changed between versions and make upgrade decisions easier.

### Motivation
When upgrading dependencies, developers need to know:
- What bugs were fixed
- What new features were added
- Whether there are any breaking changes

### Suggested Format
Follow the [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com) convention:

```markdown
# Changelog

## [Unreleased]

## [1.2.0] - 2024-01-15
### Added
- New feature X
### Fixed  
- Bug with Y under Z conditions
### Changed
- Behaviour of Z is now more consistent
```

### Additional Context
This is purely a documentation change with no code impact.

title: PERF: Pure Python loops when calculating validity masks and offset arrays in Interchange Protocol
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Currently, when exporting string columns via the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas processes the validity mask and offset buffers using slow element-wise Python loops:

```python
# Validity Mask loop
mask = np.zeros(shape=(len(buf),), dtype=np.bool_)
for i, obj in enumerate(buf):
    mask[i] = valid if isinstance(obj, str) else invalid

# Offsets loop
for i, v in enumerate(values):
    if isinstance(v, str):
        b = v.encode(encoding="utf-8")
        ptr += len(b)
    offsets[i + 1] = ptr
```

These manual loops incur significant overhead on larger string arrays.

#### Proposed Optimization
We can vectorize these buffer constructions using Python list comprehensions and NumPy functions:

1. Construct the boolean validity mask via `[isinstance(obj, str) for obj in buf] `and direct array casting.
2. Accumulate string byte-lengths into a list and execute a single vectorized cumulative sum call (`np.cumsum`) to generate the offsets array.

#### Performance Benchmarks
Benchmarked on a string column with 100k rows (with 5% missing values):
| Operation | Old (Master) | New (Optimized) | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Validity Mask** | 0.188 seconds | 0.102 seconds | **1.84x** |
| **Offsets Buffer** | 0.421 seconds | 0.267 seconds | **1.57x** |

title: PERF: High overhead in stack frame warning inspections (find_stack_level)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Whenever pandas raises a warning, it invokes `find_stack_level()` to trace the call stack and identify the calling context outside of pandas. Currently, this function walks the stack frames and calls `inspect.getfile(frame)` inside a loop:

```python
while frame:
    filename = inspect.getfile(frame)
    if filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir):
        frame = frame.f_back
        n += 1
```

For workloads that emit multiple warnings (or libraries relying heavily on pandas warnings), this function is highly inefficient because:
1. `inspect.getfile(frame)` is slow as it does lookup caching, module parsing, and absolute path validation inside the interpreter loop.
2. It repeatedly imports `pandas` and resolves `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths on *every* warning invocation.

### Proposed Optimization
1. Cache the `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths globally at the module level.
2. Retrieve the filename directly via `frame.f_code.co_filename` instead of calling `inspect.getfile(frame)`.

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked 500,000 runs of the original stack inspection vs. the optimized caching and `co_filename` check on a local environment:

| Implementation | 500,000 runs | Overhead per call |
|---|---|---|
| **Original (`master`)** | 3.67 seconds | ~7.33 microseconds |
| **Optimized** | 0.19 seconds | ~0.38 microseconds |

This yields a **~19x speedup** (95% reduction in call overhead).

title: PERF: High overhead in DataFrame.apply(raw=True) due to np.apply_along_axis

### Problem Description
When calling `DataFrame.apply(..., raw=True)` with the default Python engine (non-Numba), pandas currently delegates array execution to `numpy.apply_along_axis`. 

While `np.apply_along_axis` is generic and supports arbitrary N-dimensional arrays, it introduces significant Python-level overhead (dynamic coordinate tuple creation, slice-by-slice writes, first-element inspection to determine dtype). Since DataFrame values are strictly 2D, we can optimize this execution path by using a fast-path list comprehension and transposition logic, which yields a **1.4x to 2.2x** performance improvement.

* **Row-wise Apply (`axis=1`):** 0.0437s down to 0.0306s (**1.43x speedup**)

title: PERF: String column serialization in Interchange protocol is slow
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


### Problem Description
Currently, when serializing string columns to a byte buffer in the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas uses a slow element-wise Python loop:

```python
for obj in buf:
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        b.extend(obj.encode(encoding="utf-8"))
```

For large DataFrames ($100k+$ or $1M+$ rows), this loop is highly inefficient because:
1. It calls `.encode("utf-8")` once for every single string element inside the Python interpreter.
2. It uses `bytearray.extend()` iteratively, introducing overhead.
3. The check `isinstance(obj, str)` is run iteratively in Python.

### Proposed Optimization
We can leverage NumPy to filter nulls/invalid elements in C-space and then perform a single C-optimized join and a single vectorized `.encode()` call:

```python
# Drop null values to avoid joining None/NaN
b = "".join(buf[pd.notna(buf)]).encode(encoding="utf-8")
```

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked the original loop logic vs. the optimized NumPy mask & join approach on array sizes with 5% missing values:

| Size (Strings) | Original Loop | Optimized Python | Speedup Factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **10,000** | 0.00530s | 0.00227s | **2.34x** |
| **100,000** | 0.06940s | 0.02344s | **2.96x** |
| **1,000,000** | 0.22295s | 0.10143s | **2.20x** |

title: BUG: CustomBusinessMonthBegin and CustomBusinessMonthEnd type signatures are missing the calendar and weekmask keyword arguments
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

cal = np.busdaycalendar()

pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin(calendar=cal)
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd(calendar=cal)
```

### Issue Description

## Description

The type signatures for `CustomBusinessMonthBegin` and `CustomBusinessMonthEnd` are missing the `calendar` and `weekmask` keyword arguments, even though they are supported at runtime and documented.

By comparison, `CustomBusinessDay` correctly exposes the `calendar` parameter in its type signature.

As a result, valid code fails type checking with mypy.

## Reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

cal = np.busdaycalendar()

pd.offsets.CustomBusinessDay(calendar=cal)          # OK
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin(calendar=cal)   # mypy error
pd.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd(calendar=cal)     # mypy error
```

mypy reports:

```text
error: Unexpected keyword argument "calendar" for "CustomBusinessMonthBegin"  [call-arg]
error: Unexpected keyword argument "calendar" for "CustomBusinessMonthEnd"  [call-arg]
```

## `reveal_type`

```python
from pandas.tseries.offsets import (
    CustomBusinessDay,
    CustomBusinessMonthBegin,
    CustomBusinessMonthEnd,
)

reveal_type(CustomBusinessDay)
reveal_type(CustomBusinessMonthBegin)
reveal_type(CustomBusinessMonthEnd)
```

Output:

```text
Revealed type is "def (
    n: int =,
    normalize: bool =,
    holidays: list[Any] =,
    calendar: pandas.tseries.holiday.AbstractHolidayCalendar | numpy._core.multiarray.busdaycalendar =
) -> pandas._libs.tslibs.offsets.CustomBusinessDay"

Revealed type is "def (
    n: int =,
    normalize: bool =,
    offset: datetime.timedelta =,
    holidays: list[Any] | None =
) -> pandas._libs.tslibs.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin"

Revealed type is "def (
    n: int =,
    normalize: bool =,
    offset: datetime.timedelta =,
    holidays: list[Any] | None =
) -> pandas._libs.tslibs.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd"
```

Notably, the month offset signatures are missing both `calendar` and `weekmask`.

## Expected behavior

The type signatures for `CustomBusinessMonthBegin` and `CustomBusinessMonthEnd` should match the documented/runtime API and accept the same customization parameters as the runtime implementation, including:

- `calendar`
- `weekmask`
- `holidays`

## Environment

- pandas 3.0.3
- mypy 2.1.0

### Documentation

The official documentation lists the `calendar` parameter:

- https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.tseries.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthBegin.html
- https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.tseries.offsets.CustomBusinessMonthEnd.html

title: BUG: `pivot_table` with `margins=True` raises KeyError when dict aggfunc doesn't cover every aggregated column
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/development/contributing_environment.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "random1": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        "random2": [10, 20, 30, 40],
        "type": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
    }
)

# aggfunc only covers "random1"; "random2" is picked up implicitly via `values`
df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

### Issue Description

Raises:

```
KeyError: 'random2'
```

Without `margins=True`, the exact same call works fine and silently excludes `random2` from the result (since it isn't a key in the `aggfunc` dict):

```python
>>> df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"})
      random1
type
a         1.5
b         3.5
```

This also reproduces when `values` is passed explicitly and includes a column not covered by the dict:

```python
df.pivot_table(index="type", values=["random1", "random2"], aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

The root cause seems to be in `_compute_grand_margin` in `pandas/core/reshape/pivot.py`: it iterates over every column in `data[values]` and looks up `aggfunc[k]` for each one. When `aggfunc` is a dict that doesn't have a key for `k`, this will raise a `KeyError`, which propagates uncaught (only `TypeError` is currently swallowed there). I guess the fix is to skip columns not present in the dict, consistent with the non-margins aggregation path's existing (if implicit) behavior of silently dropping such columns.

I found as an incidental, separate issue while investigating and trying to fix #12210 on my own (dict `aggfunc` containing a list of functions per column + `margins=True`). However, this is a distinct root cause/code path and reproduces independently of list-vs-scalar functions.

### Expected Behavior

`margins=True` should produce the same set of columns as `margins=False` (i.e. silently drop columns the `aggfunc` dict doesn't cover), rather than raising `KeyError`.

### Installed Versions

main branch (post `84d7518bdc`)

title: BUG: `Series.to_json()` wraps `np.uint64` values ≥ `2**63` when stored in `object` dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype=object).to_json()
# '{"0":-9223372036854775808}'
```

### Issue Description

**Expected Output for Reproducible Example**

```python
'{"0":9223372036854775808}'
```

**Observed Behavior**

It appears that `np.uint64` scalars stored in `object`-dtype Series are being serialized through a signed `int64` path, causing values ≥ `2**63` to wrap to negative numbers.

```python
>>> pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype="uint64").to_json()
'{"0":9223372036854775808}'

>>> pd.Series([np.uint64(2**63)], dtype=object).to_json()
'{"0":-9223372036854775808}'
```

**Existing tests and documentation**

- `ujson.ujson_dumps` explicitly tests Python integers up to `18446744073709551615` (`2**64 - 1`) and expects exact JSON output. [[ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py#L540)
- `DataFrame.to_json` has a test for large uint64-looking values like `13342205958987758245`, and expects them to serialize correctly. [[ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_pandas.py#L2326)
- The docs for `to_json`/`read_json` do not appear to say "ujson only encodes up to signed int64." [[read_json ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/io/json/_json.py#L535) [[to_json ref]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/io/json/_json.py#L139)

There is one internal test comment in `pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py:718`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/tests/io/json/test_ujson.py#L712-L726

But that test is only avoiding `np.uint64.max` in a numpy-scalar roundtrip test. This suggests the object-scalar path may already have a known limitation around `np.uint64` values.

**Debugging Hints**

From debugging, it appears the object-scalar serialization path may be converting `np.uint64` values using the signed integer conversion (`NPY_INT64`) rather than the unsigned path (`NPY_UINT64`).

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/f7246dccfaca04609d03820636b0caedf30672fb/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L1627-L1631


If this is confirmed as a bug, I’d be happy to help work on a fix and open a pull request.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.to_json()` should preserve the value of `np.uint64` scalars regardless of whether they are stored in a `uint64` Series or an `object` Series.

### Installed Versions

<details>

pandas==3.1.0.dev0+1194.gf7246dccfa

</details>

title: ENH: Enable LSan in CI
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

#65812 enabled ASan and UBsan in CI, but it doesn't detect memory leaks due to `detect_leaks=0`. AFAIU, the main idea of adding ASan in CI from #52990 was to detect memory leaks. 

### Feature Description

The ASan/UBsan job needs to be updated to detect memory leaks. Unfortunately, it's not as simple as setting `detect_leaks=1` because it will contain several false positives and suppressing `libpython` will ignore real memory leaks.

From my experience, it's best to build CPython from source with `--with-address-sanitizer --without-pymalloc` and the LSan becomes a lot better: fewer false positives and simpler suppression files.

AFAIK, it's not possible to use Pixi to manage Python dependencies from a custom interpreter, so probably will have to install python dependencies via `pip` or something similar.

### Alternative Solutions

See #52990.

### Additional Context

### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

import pandas as pd
s1=pd.Series([2,9], index=['a','b'])
s2=pd.Series([11,7], index=['b','a'])
s3=s1+s2
print(s3)

s4=s1>s2
print(s4)

When performing addition between two series object pandas searches for matching index in both and does the evaluation. If any one value is missing then it it gives nan.

But compared to arithmetic , the relational operators(>,<, <=,>=, etc) are having strict requirement that the order of the index must match. In the code above indexes a and b are both present in s1 and s2 and s1>s2 can be done as both indexes are present in both s1 and s2 but currently it is not allowed as there is a strict requirement that for relational operators the order of the indexes must also match.

It would be intutive if the requirement of index order is relaxed for relational operators and only matching index is checked.

title: Add type hints to public API functions
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
Adding type hints to public API functions would significantly improve developer experience and enable better tooling support.

### Motivation
- IDEs can provide better autocomplete and inline documentation
- Static type checkers like `mypy` can catch bugs before runtime
- New contributors can understand the expected inputs/outputs faster
- Type hints serve as machine-checked documentation

### Proposed Change
Add type annotations to all public functions:

```python
# Before:
def process(data, config=None):
    ...

# After:
from typing import Optional, Dict, Any

def process(data: Dict[str, Any], config: Optional[Dict] = None) -> bool:
    ...
```

### Additional Context
This is a non-breaking change and can be done incrementally, starting with the most-used public functions.

title: BUG: pd.date_range(freq='h') produces astronomically large freq on Python 3.14, causing OverflowError
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/v3.0.4.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
print(pd.__version__)   # 3.0.4
print(pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h"))
```

### Issue Description

On **pandas 3.0.4 + Python 3.14**, `pd.date_range(..., freq="h")` raises an `OverflowError` / `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`. The `freq` argument is silently reinterpreted as an astronomically large `Hours` offset (e.g. `<281467879224592 * Hours>`) instead of `<1 * Hours>`.

The same call works correctly on **pandas 3.0.3 + Python 3.14**.

### Full traceback

```
pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.pyx:2014: OverflowError

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

start = Timestamp('2026-04-17 00:00:00'), end = None, periods = 24
freq = <281467879224592 * Hours>, unit = 'us'

    def generate_regular_range(...):
        ...
        try:
            td = td.as_unit(unit, round_ok=False)
        except ValueError as err:
            raise ValueError(
                f"freq={freq} is incompatible with unit={unit}. "
                "Use a lower freq or a higher unit instead."
            ) from err

pandas/core/arrays/_ranges.py:74: ValueError:

```

Also observed as:

```
pandas.errors.OutOfBoundsTimedelta:
  Cannot cast 11727828301024 days 16:00:00 to unit='us' without overflow.
```

### Expected Behavior

`pd.date_range("2026-04-17 00:00", periods=24, freq="h")` should return a `DatetimeIndex` of 24 hourly timestamps, as it does on pandas 3.0.3.

### Installed Versions

- pandas: **3.0.4** (regression; **3.0.3** works)
- Python: **3.14.6**

Note: `freq="h"` (lowercase) is the recommended alias since pandas 2.2 (replacing the deprecated `"H"`), so this is not a deprecated-alias issue.

title: BUG: Segfault constructing pd.Timedelta on Python 3.14 (pandas 3.0.4, regression from 3.0.3)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

In a fresh virtualenv with **only** `pandas==3.0.4` (and its required deps `numpy`, `python-dateutil`) installed on **CPython 3.14**:

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Timedelta(days=28)   # Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
```

Any `Timedelta` constructor crashes the interpreter at construction time — `pd.Timedelta(days=28)`, `pd.Timedelta("28 days")`, `pd.Timedelta(28, "D")`. No DataFrame/Series is involved, no threading, single-threaded `python -c`.

### Issue Description

Constructing a `pandas.Timedelta` segfaults immediately on **pandas 3.0.4 / CPython 3.14**. This is a **regression from 3.0.3** — in the same virtualenv, downgrading only `pandas` (`3.0.4` → `3.0.3`, numpy unchanged) makes the example work, and upgrading back to `3.0.4` crashes again. So `pandas` is the only changed variable.

It reproduces with numpy **2.3.3** (pandas 3.0.4's own declared minimum for Python 3.14, `numpy>=2.3.3`) and with numpy **2.4.6**, so it is not specific to a single numpy build.

With `PYTHONFAULTHANDLER=1`, the C stack shows what looks like unbounded recursion between `pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas` and numpy's `_multiarray_umath`, overflowing the C stack:

```
Current thread's C stack trace (most recent call first):
  ...python... _Py_DumpStack
  /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6(+0x45330)
  numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x101f18)
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x541ac)
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x590ac)
  python _PyObject_MakeTpCall+0x1e7
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x51f12)   # (deeper frames repeat the
  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so(+0x590ac)   #  timedeltas +0x590ac <-> MakeTpCall pattern)
  python _PyObject_MakeTpCall+0x1e7
  ...
```

The Python-level stack is just the single `pd.Timedelta(...)` call line — the fault is entirely in the compiled extension.

I haven't bisected which 3.0.4 commit introduced it, but the only `_libs` source change between 3.0.3 and 3.0.4 that touches this area is the datetime C code (e.g. the `np_datetime.c` include-order change, #65591/#65609); the maintainers will know best where to look.

### Expected Behavior

`pd.Timedelta(days=28)` returns `Timedelta('28 days 00:00:00')`, as it does on pandas 3.0.3.

Note: this currently makes pandas 3.0.4 unusable for any downstream library that constructs a `Timedelta` at import time (e.g. importing RAPIDS cuDF segfaults for this reason).

I have only been able to test CPython **3.14.6** so far (couldn't easily build other interpreters in this environment); I don't yet know whether 3.11–3.13 are affected.

title: BUG: pd.to_datetime segfaults on Series of duplicated ISO8601 strings (regression in 3.0.4)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/pandas/) of pandas (3.0.4).
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas. (Reproduced on the latest released 3.0.4; happy to retest on main if a wheel/build is provided.)

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# 50 unique ISO8601 timestamp strings, repeated up to 3000 rows
base = [f"2000-01-01T0{i % 9}:00:00.000" for i in range(50)]
vals = [base[i % len(base)] for i in range(3000)]

pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(vals))   # Segmentation fault (core dumped) on 3.0.4
print("SUCCESS - no segfault")
```

Run with `python -X faulthandler repro.py`.

### Issue Description

`pd.to_datetime()` on a `Series` of duplicated ISO8601 timestamp strings **segfaults** (process dies with `Segmentation fault (core dumped)`, exit code 139) on **pandas 3.0.4**. There is no Python exception; the interpreter crashes in native code.

The crash requires:
- A sufficiently large series (reproduces at ~3000 rows; does **not** reproduce at ~2000), and
- Many duplicate values (the input factorizes to a small number of unique timestamps, which routes through the `map_array` / `take` fast path).

title: BUG: Segfault constructing pd.Timedelta with numpy 2.3.x/2.4.x on Python 3.14 (pandas 3.0.4)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas (3.0.4).

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.Timedelta(1, unit="D")   # interpreter exits with SIGSEGV (signal 11)
```

`import pandas` succeeds; `numpy.timedelta64(1, "D")` succeeds; the **first**
`pd.Timedelta(...)` construction crashes the interpreter. No Python traceback is
produced.

### Issue Description

On Python 3.14, `pandas==3.0.4` segfaults when constructing a `Timedelta` if the
installed numpy is in the 2.3.x–2.4.x range. The crash is a hard SIGSEGV
(exit 139), single-process and fully deterministic.

The numpy `_multiarray_umath` shared object is not stripped, so the faulting
frame symbolizes exactly:

```
#0  PyUFunc_f_f (numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so + 0xd5f58)
        => mov (%rdx),%r15            # registers at fault: rdx = 0x6, rcx = 0x0
#1  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#2  pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
#3  slot_tp_new -> type_call -> _PyObject_MakeTpCall    # Timedelta(1, unit='D')
```

`PyUFunc_f_f` is numpy's generic float32 unary ufunc inner loop, whose signature
is `(char **args, npy_intp *dimensions, npy_intp *steps, void *func)`. At the
fault, `rdx` (the `steps` pointer) holds `0x6` and `rcx` (`func`) is `NULL`; the
loop dereferences `steps` and segfaults.

I bisected across numpy/pandas versions, each in a clean venv (Python 3.14.5),
running only the one-liner above:

| numpy  | pandas | result  |
|--------|--------|---------|
| 2.3.5  | 3.0.3  | OK      |
| 2.3.5  | 3.0.4  | SIGSEGV |
| 2.4.6  | 3.0.4  | SIGSEGV |
| 2.5.0  | 3.0.4  | OK      |

Observations (reporting only, not asserting a cause):

- pandas 3.0.3 and 3.0.4 both declare `numpy>=2.3.3; python_version >= "3.14"`.
  3.0.3 runs fine on numpy 2.3.5; 3.0.4 segfaults on the same numpy.
- 3.0.4 runs fine on numpy 2.5.0 but segfaults on numpy 2.3.5 and 2.4.6.
- Reproduced on three different x86-64 CPUs/hosts (one with AVX2, one without)
  and inside a `python3.14` Debian-bookworm container — so it does not appear to
  be CPU- or host-specific.

### Expected Behavior

`pd.Timedelta(1, unit="D")` returns a `Timedelta` (or raises a Python exception)
rather than segfaulting, for any numpy version permitted by pandas's declared
dependency metadata.

### Installed Versions

<details>

```
python : 3.14.5 (x86_64, glibc 2.42)
pandas : 3.0.4   (manylinux x86_64 wheel, PyPI)
numpy  : 2.3.5   (manylinux x86_64 wheel, PyPI)
OS     : Linux 7.0.12 (Fedora 43); also reproduced on Debian bookworm container
install: clean venv -> `pip install numpy==2.3.5 pandas==3.0.4`
```

</details>

title: BUG: to_html with render_links=True and escape=True does not escape the href attribute
body:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python import pandas as pd value = 'http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en' html = pd.DataFrame({"url": [value]}).to_html(render_links=True, escape=True) print(html) assert "http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en" in html assert 'href="http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en"' in html ``` ### Issue Description `DataFrame.to_html(render_links=True, escape=True)` escapes the visible cell text, but the generated `href` attribute uses the original cell value without the same HTML escaping. The relevant implementation is in `pandas/io/formats/html.py`: ```python rs = pprint_thing(s, escape_chars=esc).strip() if self.render_links and is_url(rs): rs_unescaped = pprint_thing(s, escape_chars={}).strip() start_tag += f'' ``` With the value from the example above, the visible cell text is escaped as expected, but the `href` attribute keeps the raw double quote and ampersand. The generated table therefore has different escaping behavior between the visible URL text and the generated link URL. Current generated output includes this shape: ```html http://example.com/search?q=a"b&lang=en ``` This is surprising because `escape=True` changes the visible text to `"` and `&`, while `render_links=True` keeps the raw characters in the generated `href`. ### Expected Behavior When `escape=True` and `render_links=True` are both enabled, the generated anchor should apply consistent HTML escaping to the URL value before placing it in `href`. For example, the generated output should represent the same URL value consistently in both the anchor's `href` attribute and the visible link text. ### Installed Versions
Directly visible environment information: - pandas: 3.0.3 - Python container image: python:3.13-slim
Reproduced with pandas `3.0.3`. The same `rs_unescaped` implementation is also present on the current `main` branch at `pandas/io/formats/html.py`.

title: BUG: Series.str.match returns wrong result for ^a|b patterns on string[pyarrow] dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
python 

import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["xbar", "bar", "foo", "xfoo"])

print("Actual:  ", s.str.match(r"^foo|bar").tolist())
print("Expected:", s.astype(object).str.match(r"^foo|bar").tolist())





Output 
Actual:   [True, True, True, False]
Expected: [False, True, True, False]
```

### Issue Description

`Series.str.match(r"^foo|bar")` on the default (PyArrow-backed) string dtype silently returns True for "xbar" (matches "bar" at position 1 instead of requiring it at position 0), because the ^ only anchors the first alternation branch.

Object dtype (and `re.match`) anchors the whole pattern at position 0 and correctly returns False, so this is a silent regression for users on pandas 3.x with PyArrow installed.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.str.match(pat)` should anchor the entire pattern at position 0 (matching Python's `re.match` and the object-dtype behavior), so `r"^foo|bar"` should only return `True` for strings that start with `"foo"` or `"bar"`.

title: DataFrame constructed from Index or Series mutates the original object
body:
# BUG: `DataFrame` constructed from `Index` or `Series` mutates the original object

## Description

When constructing a `DataFrame` from a pandas `Index` or `Series` containing string data, any modifications made to the new `DataFrame` unexpectedly mutate the original `Index` or `Series`. This occurs even when `.copy()` is explicitly called before passing the object to the constructor — the underlying array is reused rather than being independently tracked.

This bug does **not** affect integer-backed `Index` or `Series` objects, only string (and other extension array) types.

Additionally, this can break internal invariants — displaying a `DataFrame` whose columns were modified this way has been observed to crash the IPython kernel.

## Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# Bug with Index input
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
columns = pd.DataFrame(data=df.columns.copy())
columns.loc[0, 0] = 'C'
assert df.columns[0] == 'A'  # FAILS — original Index was mutated

# Bug with string Index directly
idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"])
df2 = pd.DataFrame(idx)
df2.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(idx)  # Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original mutated

# Bug with string Series input
ser = pd.Series(["A", "B"])
df3 = pd.DataFrame(ser)
df3.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(ser)  # 0    C \n 1    B — original mutated

# No bug with integer Index (works correctly)
idx_int = pd.Index([0, 1])
df4 = pd.DataFrame(idx_int)
df4.iloc[0, 0] = 100
print(idx_int)  # Index([0, 1], dtype='int64') — unchanged
```

## Expected Behavior

```python
idx = pd.Index(["A", "B"])
df = pd.DataFrame(idx)
df.iloc[0, 0] = "C"
print(idx)  # Expected: Index(['A', 'B'], dtype='str') — unchanged
```

## Actual Behavior

```python
print(idx)  # Actual: Index(['C', 'B'], dtype='str') — original was silently mutated
```

```
pandas     : 3.1.0.dev0+37.g98ffe4c45e

python     : 3.11.14

```python
import pandas as pd

columns = pd.DataFrame(data=df.columns.copy())

assert df.columns[0] == 'A'  # fails — it's 'C'

If you build a `DataFrame` from an `Index` or `Series` backed by an Extension Array, CoW reference tracking is missing. The result is that mutating the new `DataFrame` can silently change the original `Index` — which obviously shouldn't happen.

On top of that, we ran into IPython kernel crashes when trying to display a `DataFrame` whose columns had been modified this way, which suggests some internal block manager invariants are getting broken too.


### Expected Behavior

`df.columns` shouldn't be affected at all. CoW means either copy the data upfront or track the reference and copy on first write — neither is happening here.

s == "a"

```

### Issue Description

Following doc, the pandas.Categorical represent a categorical variable in classic R / S-plus fashion.

However comparison to missingness (== or !=) is handled differently.

```
# python
>>> s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "a", pd.NA], dtype="category")
... s == "a"

0     True
1    False
2     True
3    False
dtype: bool

# r
> s <- factor(c("a", "b", "a", NA))
> s == "a"
[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE    NA
```

### Expected Behavior

In the chunk above last element of pd.Series is False, where should be pd.NA for consistency (with R and intuition/logic)

If possible, I'd suggest to make this consistent to R (both for newcomers and to avoid boilerplate code after comparison of any categorical). Otherwise I'd suggest to notice this in: 

https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/categorical.html#differences-to-r-s-factor

Many thanks as always, best

title: Add logging support for better observability
body:
## Feature Request

### Summary
The project would benefit from structured logging to make it easier to debug issues in production.

### Motivation
Currently it can be difficult to understand what the application is doing at runtime without adding print statements. Proper logging would:

- Allow users to control verbosity with log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)
- Make it easier to integrate with log aggregation systems
- Help diagnose issues in production without code changes

### Proposed Implementation
```python
import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def my_function():
    log.debug("Starting my_function")
    # ... 
    log.info("my_function completed successfully")
```

### Impact
Low risk change with high value for users running this in production environments.

title: BUG: Plotting with timezone-aware and normalized `DatetimeIndex` drops tz-info
body:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python from matplotlib import ( axes as maxes, pyplot as plt, dates as mdates, ) import pandas as pd # Create a figure with two subplots fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows=2, figsize=(8, 10), sharex=False) def print_sr_line_comparison(sr, line): print(f"{sr.name}:") print(f"{sr.index.is_normalized=}", end="\n\n") print("Series:", sr, "", "Line Data:", line.get_xdata(), "", sep="\n", end="\n\n") # Create two Series with timezone-aware DatetimeIndex, one in EST and one in UTC idx_est = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-02 00:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-03 00:00:00-06:00"]) idx_utc = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-02 00:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-03 00:00:00+00:00"]) sr_est = pd.Series(range(len(idx_est)), index=idx_est, name="EST") sr_utc = pd.Series(range(len(idx_utc)), index=idx_utc, name="UTC") + 0.2 # Plot both Series on the first subplot sr_est.plot(ax=ax[0], marker="o") sr_utc.plot(ax=ax[0], marker="s") ax[0].title.set_text("Series with regularly spaced timestamps in index") # Print comparison of Series and Line data for the first subplot print("1. Figure\n") print_sr_line_comparison(sr_est, ax[0].lines[0]) print_sr_line_comparison(sr_utc, ax[0].lines[1]) print("-----------------------------------\n\n\n") # Add an additional in index non-regular datapoint to each Series sr_est.loc["2000-01-02 12:00:00-06:00"] = 1.5 sr_est.sort_index(inplace=True) sr_utc.loc["2000-01-02 12:00:00+00:00"] = 1.7 sr_utc.sort_index(inplace=True) # Plot both Series on the second subplot ax[1].title.set_text("Series with additional non-regular datapoint") sr_est.plot(ax=ax[1], marker="o") sr_utc.plot(ax=ax[1], marker="s") # Print comparison of Series and Line data for the first subplot print("2. Figure\n") print_sr_line_comparison(sr_est, ax[1].lines[0]) print_sr_line_comparison(sr_utc, ax[1].lines[1]) print("-----------------------------------\n\n\n") # Just some formatting to have similar x-axis for axes in ax: axes: maxes.Axes axes.legend() axes.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.DayLocator(tz="UTC")) axes.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y-%m-%d")) axes.xaxis.set_minor_locator(mdates.HourLocator(interval=6, tz="UTC")) axes.set_xlim(pd.Timestamp("2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00"), pd.Timestamp("2000-01-04 00:00:00+00:00")) axes.grid(True, which="major", linestyle="-", linewidth=1) axes.grid(True, which="minor", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.5) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ### Issue Description While writing tests for the plotting of ExtensionArrays (#64535) I noticed that under certain circumstances a `DatetimeIndex` used for the x-axis is converted to `Period` and thereby is losing the timezone information. This seems to be only happing if the `DatetimeIndex` is normalized (i.e. a frequency `freq` can be determinated) and if the `DatetimeIndex` aligns perfectly with `Period`, e.g. time is midnight/`00:00:00` for day frequency or time is on the full hour/`xx:00:00` for hourly. As a result of the loss of timezone information different Series with same "native time", but different timezone, e.g. the Series above with `EST` respectively `UTC` timezone, are plotted at the same times (top plot), whereas in reality the datapoints should be separated by 6 hours. On the contrary Series with non-normalized `DatetimeIndex` or a not-aligned one are correctly plotted (bottom plot):
Full debug printing output of the example above ```python 1. Figure EST: sr.index.is_normalized=True Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00 0 2000-01-02 00:00:00-06:00 1 2000-01-03 00:00:00-06:00 2 Name: EST, dtype: int64 Line Data: [Period('2000-01-01', 'D') Period('2000-01-02', 'D') Period('2000-01-03', 'D')] UTC: sr.index.is_normalized=True Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00 0.2 2000-01-02 00:00:00+00:00 1.2 2000-01-03 00:00:00+00:00 2.2 Name: UTC, dtype: float64 Line Data: [Period('2000-01-01', 'D') Period('2000-01-02', 'D') Period('2000-01-03', 'D')] ----------------------------------- 2. Figure EST: sr.index.is_normalized=False Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00 0.0 2000-01-02 00:00:00-06:00 1.0 2000-01-02 12:00:00-06:00 1.5 2000-01-03 00:00:00-06:00 2.0 Name: EST, dtype: float64 Line Data: [Timestamp('2000-01-01 00:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00') Timestamp('2000-01-02 00:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00') Timestamp('2000-01-02 12:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00') Timestamp('2000-01-03 00:00:00-0600', tz='UTC-06:00')] UTC: sr.index.is_normalized=False Series: 2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00 0.2 2000-01-02 00:00:00+00:00 1.2 2000-01-02 12:00:00+00:00 1.7 2000-01-03 00:00:00+00:00 2.2 Name: UTC, dtype: float64 Line Data: [Timestamp('2000-01-01 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC') Timestamp('2000-01-02 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC') Timestamp('2000-01-02 12:00:00+0000', tz='UTC') Timestamp('2000-01-03 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC')] ```
As it can be seen in the example/graphic, adding the additional datapoint to the Series for the bottom plot, changes also the positions of all other data points as the `DatetimeIndex` is not anymore normalized. The `LineData` printed during the execution also confirms the transformation of the Series to list of `Period` objects for the first plot, while in the second plot they are transformed to a list of timezone aware `Timestamp` objects. The issue seems to come from the [`use_dynamic_x` function](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/644bf599e420c43960c26fa6225745a14f7ef156/pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/timeseries.py#L249) which determinates if `DatetimeIndex` can be converted to `Period`, but apparently failing to do so. There also was a PR recently (#63013) dealing with timezone-aware data and this function, but it has gone stale since and I do not think it would solve the issue here as the path with `index[:1].is_normalized` is not changed. I think there are also some similarities to #15754, but there were only the tick locations affected and not the data. I also do not see a common code path (anymore), but I did not dig into the issue there and if it still persists. @jbrockmendel You recently changed the comments in `use_dynamic_x` in 95405ddd7d7fefb0a05f6f271529009c201cd463 and reviewed the other PR, do you have an opinion how this should be handled? @jorisvandenbossche You commented on the other issue, maybe you also have an opinion on the topic, on the hand that one is already 7 years old, so no issue if not. While I was writing the example I also noticed the following, but not sure how they relate: 1. When I use hourly data like the following two indices then I get super weird date labels, instead of something around `2000-01-01` I got `2689-12-25` and the following days. ```python idx_est = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-01 01:00:00-06:00", "2000-01-01 02:00:00-06:00"]) idx_utc = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2000-01-01 00:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-01 01:00:00+00:00", "2000-01-01 02:00:00+00:00"]) ``` 2. Forcing alignment between both plots with `sharex=True`, makes the added datapoint in the bottom plot to jump from `2000-01-02 12:00:00` to `2000-01-02 00:00:00`, my first guess is the data is converted by the `PeriodConverter` set for the x-axis to the first axes (top plot) and as the frequency is `day` only mightnight values are valid. ### Expected Behavior The location of data points on the x-axis should be independent from the `DatetimeIndex` being normalized or not. It also leads very quickly to plainly wrong plots if different time zones are involved. With the data in the example I would always expect to get the horizontal displacement between the two Series of different time zone in a common plot like it is shown in the bottom plot. I am not sure if it makes sense to keep the whole `use_dynamic_x` function or if it can be reformed somehow. The biggest issue seems to be the first Series is normalized so it registers a `PeriodConverter` to that axis, but then the second Series might be a non normalized `DatetimeIndex` or has a different time zone, but is forced into the Periods defined by the first Series. ### Installed Versions
INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit : 0cdc017c38ba23a6f1759ecaf6d4bf4835fad086 python : 3.11.15 python-bits : 64 OS : Linux OS-release : 5.15.153.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2 Version : #1 SMP Fri Mar 29 23:14:13 UTC 2024 machine : x86_64 processor : x86_64 byteorder : little LC_ALL : None LANG : C.UTF-8 LOCALE : en_US.UTF-8 pandas : 3.1.0.dev0+641.g0cdc017c38 numpy : 2.4.3 dateutil : 2.9.0.post0 pip : 26.0.1 Cython : 3.2.4 sphinx : 9.0.4 IPython : 9.10.1 adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite : None bs4 : 4.14.3 bottleneck : 1.6.0 fastparquet : 2025.12.0 fsspec : 2026.2.0 html5lib : 1.1 hypothesis : 6.151.11 gcsfs : 2026.2.0 jinja2 : 3.1.6 lxml.etree : 6.0.2 matplotlib : 3.10.8 numba : 0.65.0 numexpr : 2.14.1 odfpy : None openpyxl : 3.1.5 psycopg2 : 2.9.11 pymysql : 1.4.6 pyarrow : 23.0.1 pyiceberg : 0.11.1 pyreadstat : 1.3.3 pytest : 9.0.3 python-calamine : None pytz : 2026.1.post1 pyxlsb : 1.0.10 s3fs : 2026.2.0 scipy : 1.17.1 sqlalchemy : 2.0.49 tables : 3.11.1 tabulate : 0.10.0 xarray : 2026.2.0 xlrd : 2.0.2 xlsxwriter : 3.2.9 zstandard : 0.25.0 qtpy : None pyqt5 : None

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

branches = pd.DataFrame(
    data={
        "name": ["river_1", "river_2", "river_3", "river_4", "river_4-1", "pipe_51_E11", "pipe_51_E12", "pipe_52_E0"],
        "branchtype": [0,0,0,0,0,2,2,2],
        "sourceCompartmentName": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, "manhole_987_generated", "manhole_988_generated", "manhole_989_generated"],
        "targetCompartmentName": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, "manhole_988_generated",
                                  "manhole_967_generated", "manhole_990_generated"],
    },
index=[0,1,2,3,4,1002,1003,1004],
)

# print the dtype, str in pandas 2 (?) and <StringDtype(na_value=nan)> in pandas 3
# using repr since StringDtype is also printed as str otherwise
print(branches["sourceCompartmentName"].dtype.__repr__())

# does not work in pandas 3, since None is interpreted as the dype na_value
branches = branches.replace(np.nan, None)
# a useful workaround that does work
# branches = branches.replace([np.nan], [None])

print(branches.to_dict("records"))
```

### Issue Description

Context: Originally reported in https://github.com/Deltares/HYDROLIB-core/issues/1107. In our code, we would regularly initiating an object of some class (hydrolib-core BranchModel) with some parameters set to `None`. These are then considered empty/notset, consistent with many other class/method argument defaults.

This is why we need to have `None` values in our dataframes with string dtype columns (and not np.nan values). Pandas 2 supports both these values, pandas 3 implemented stringdtype to be more robust. This has a na_value argument/property, which is set to np.nan per default. This na_value cannot be set to `None` since it is considered an empty argument (which sort of makes sense to me).

However, we noticed that in pandas 3 it is actually possible to convert `np.nan` to `None`  by adding square brackets:
- `branches.replace(np.nan, None)` does not replace the np.nan values
- `branches.replace([np.nan], [None])` replaces the np.nan values with None

This is quite nice for our usecase, since we can use this as a workaround. However, this seems inconsistent and might be considered as a bug. If this is intended behaviour, that is also fine since we can then trust that the behaviour will not change in the future.

### Expected Behavior

One of these two:
- consistent behaviour between the two methods
- confirmation that this is intended and will not change in the forseeable future. Or any other suggestion to avoid the need for a workaround.

title: Potential resource leak when exception occurs during file operation
body:
## Bug Report

### Description
When an exception is raised during a file operation, the file handle may not be properly closed, leading to a resource leak.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Open a file without using a context manager
2. Raise an exception before closing the file
3. The file handle remains open

### Expected Behavior
File handles should always be closed, even when exceptions occur.

### Suggested Fix
Use a `with` statement (context manager) to ensure the file is always closed:

```python
# Instead of:
f = open('file.txt', 'r')
data = f.read()
f.close()

# Use:
with open('file.txt', 'r') as f:
    data = f.read()
```

### Environment
- Python 3.x
- Any OS

This is a common Python pitfall that can cause issues in long-running applications.

title: [TEST]: Plotting tests fail with matplotlib 3.11.0 — color cycle returns RGB tuples instead of hex strings
body:
## BUG: Plotting tests fail with matplotlib 3.11.0 — color cycle returns RGB tuples instead of hex strings

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from pandas.plotting._matplotlib.style import get_standard_colors

print(f"matplotlib: {matplotlib.__version__}")  # 3.11.0
print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}")              # 3.0.3

# Returns hex strings with mpl 3.10.x, RGB tuples with mpl 3.11.0
colors = get_standard_colors(num_colors=3)
print(colors)
# mpl 3.10.9: ['#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#2ca02c']
# mpl 3.11.0: [(0.122..., 0.467..., 0.706...), (1.0, 0.498..., 0.055...), (0.173..., 0.627..., 0.173...)]

# Same issue with Line2D.get_color()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2, 3])
print(repr(line.get_color()))
# mpl 3.10.9: '#1f77b4'
# mpl 3.11.0: (0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)
plt.close()

# The colors are numerically identical:
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
print(to_hex((0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)))
# '#1f77b4'
```

### Issue Description

With matplotlib 3.11.0 (released 2026-06-12), the default property cycle now returns colors as RGB tuples rather than hex strings. This causes 5 pandas plotting tests to fail:

- `tests/plotting/test_boxplot_method.py::TestDataFramePlots::test_colors_in_theme[default-expected1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_series.py::TestSeriesPlots::test_pie_series_autopct_and_fontsize`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[1-expected_name0]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[3-expected_name1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[12-expected_name2]`

The upstream matplotlib change is https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/29469 ("Separate property cycle handling from _process_plot_var_args"), merged in commit [`ec65514`](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/commit/ec655143528f8e8dbc7897cc3c1e59865672c7ef) and released as part of [matplotlib 3.11.0](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/releases/tag/v3.11.0). This refactored the internal property cycle machinery into a dedicated class. As a side effect, the default `axes.prop_cycle` rcParam now stores colors as `(R, G, B)` float tuples rather than hex strings.

The relevant matplotlib milestone: https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/milestone/96

All affected APIs are public:
- `mpl.rcParams['axes.prop_cycle']` — iterating over the cycler now yields `{'color': (R, G, B)}` dicts instead of `{'color': '#rrggbb'}` dicts
- `Line2D.get_color()` — returns whatever format was stored in the cycle, now a tuple instead of a string

The behavior change is observable through these public APIs, though matplotlib has never formally guaranteed a specific color *format* (both hex strings and RGB tuples are valid matplotlib color specifications). The pandas tests assert a specific format (hex strings) rather than comparing semantically.

### Expected Behavior

Tests should pass with matplotlib 3.11.0. The test assertions should either:

1. Normalize colors before comparison (e.g., using `matplotlib.colors.to_hex()` or `matplotlib.colors.same_color()`), or
2. Compare in a format-agnostic way that handles both hex strings and RGB tuples.

Additionally, if `get_standard_colors()` has a documented contract about its return format, it may be worth normalizing the output within that function itself so downstream consumers aren't affected by matplotlib's internal representation changes.

### Installed Versions

<details>
<summary>Versions</summary>

- Python: 3.14
- pandas: 3.0.3
- matplotlib: 3.11.0
- numpy: 2.4.6

</details>

title: BUG: missing deprecation warning about epoch timestamps in the index in to_json()
body:
When we have a datetime64 column and writing to JSON, we get a warning about the default "epoch" `date_format` being deprecated. 
However, when the datetime64 data is in the index, we don't get the warning, while we also get epoch values:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [pd.Timestamp("2012-01-01"), pd.Timestamp("2012-01-02")]})
>>> df.to_json()
Pandas4Warning: The default 'epoch' date format is deprecated and will be removed in a future version, please use 'iso' date format instead.
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":1325376000000,"1":1325462400000}}'

>>> df.set_index("B").to_json()    # <-- no warning
'{"A":{"1325376000000":1,"1325462400000":2}}'
```

Both cases work fine with `date_format="iso"`:

```python
>>> df.to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000","1":"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000"}}'
>>> df.set_index("B").to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000":1,"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000":2}}'
```

But so if we want to be able to change to `"iso"` by default in 4.0 for both cases, we also have to warn now in both cases

title: ENH: Support %N directive in strptime parsing (to_datetime / Timestamp with format=)
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

### Problem Description

GH-29461 / PR GH-64899 added a `%N` directive to `Timestamp.strftime` and the
array-level `strftime`, formatting nanoseconds as a 9-digit zero-padded number.
The parsing side does not accept it, so `%N` output doesn't round-trip with the
same format string:

```python
>>> ts = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-14 15:32:52.192548651")
>>> fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N"
>>> pd.to_datetime(ts.strftime(fmt), format=fmt)
ValueError: 'N' is a bad directive in format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N'
```

Note that pandas' strptime already parses nanoseconds via `%f` (it accepts 1-9
digits, an extension over the stdlib's 6), so this is about symmetry and
round-tripping rather than new capability. Suggested in
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64899#pullrequestreview-4481273478.

### Feature Description

Accept `%N` in `format=` for `to_datetime`, `Timestamp`, and related parsing
paths, matching exactly 9 digits (vs `%f`'s 1-9). Likely just an entry next to
`"f"` in the `TimeRE` class and corresponding handling in `strptime.pyx`.

### Alternative Solutions

Keep parsing via `%f`, which already handles 9 digits — but then a format
string built for `%N` output can't be reused for parsing.

### Additional Context

`Period.strftime` has long supported `%n`/`%N` for formatting only; linux
`date` uses `%N` for nanoseconds.

The type information bleeds into the description:

> **quoting : {0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL,**
> 2 or csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, 3 or csv.QUOTE_NONE}, default csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL Control field quoting behavior per `csv.QUOTE_*` constants. Default is `csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL` (i.e., 0) which implies that only fields containing special characters are quoted (e.g., characters defined in `quotechar`, `delimiter`, or `lineterminator`.

### Suggested fix for documentation

It should look like this:

> **quoting : {0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL, 2 or csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, 3 or csv.QUOTE_NONE}, default csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL**
> Control field quoting behavior per `csv.QUOTE_*` constants. Default is `csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL` (i.e., 0) which implies that only fields containing special characters are quoted (e.g., characters defined in `quotechar`, `delimiter`, or `lineterminator`.

title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow engine) opens the local file path twice
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import builtins
import os

import pandas as pd

# Spy on Python-level opens of the destination path.
target = "test.parquet"
opens = []
real_open = builtins.open

def spy_open(file, *args, **kwargs):
    if os.path.abspath(os.fspath(file)) == os.path.abspath(target):
        opens.append(args)
    return real_open(file, *args, **kwargs)

builtins.open = spy_open
try:
    pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}).to_parquet(target, engine="pyarrow")
finally:
    builtins.open = real_open

print(f"pandas opened the destination {len(opens)} time(s) at the Python level")

# Observed: 1  -> pandas opens the file itself via get_handle...
# ...but pyarrow ALSO opens the same path through its C++ layer and does the
# actual writing, so the path is opened twice per to_parquet call.

# On Linux this is also visible at the syscall level:
# strace -f -e trace=openat python -c \
#  "import pandas as pd; pd.DataFrame({'a':[1]}).to_parquet('x.parquet')" 2>&1 \
#  | grep -c 'x.parquet'
# two openat() calls for the same path
```

### Issue Description

For a local filesystem path, `to_parquet` with the pyarrow engine resolves the path through `pandas.io.common.get_handle` inside `_get_path_or_handle`, then unwraps the handle's .name back to a string and hands that string to pyarrow. pyarrow then opens  the same path a second time through its own (memory-mapped, multithreaded) C++ I/O layer, which is where the read/write actually happens. So every local-path call opens the destination/source twice.

Consequences:
- On POSIX: a wasted `open()`/`close()` syscall pair on every call (minor, but pointless).
- On filesystems that finalize a file's contents when the descriptor is closed (e.g. certain write-once / object-store backed filesystems): the empty pandas-side descriptor is closed after pyarrow has written and closed its own, so the empty one wins and the file is silently truncated to 0 bytes - data loss with no error raised.

### Expected Behavior

A local path should be opened exactly once. pandas should hand the string path directly to pyarrow (which opens it itself), without first opening it via `get_handle`. The repro above should print 0 Python-level opens of the destination, and strace should show a single `openat()` for the path.

(Non-fsspec URLs such as http(s):// still need `get_handle`, since pyarrow can't fetch those - only genuine local paths should skip it.)

  apples     UInt8

  dtype: object
```

### Issue Description

  Issue Description

  When two DataFrames with nullable integer dtypes and non-overlapping columns are combined using `DataFrame.add` with a `fill_value`, columns that are absent from one of the DataFrames are silently

  s1 = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=list("abc"), dtype="UInt16")
  s2 = pd.Series([12, 22, 32], index=list("acd"), dtype="UInt16")
  print((s1 + s2).dtype)  # UInt16 — dtype preserved

title: BUG: `DataFrame.to_dict(orient="index", into=...)` does not apply `into` to nested mappings
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd


class MyDict(dict):
    pass


df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"A": [1, 2], 
    "B": ["x", "y"]}
)

out = df.to_dict("index", into=MyDict)

print(out)
print(type(out))
print(type(out[0]))

assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # fails
```

### Issue Description

Running the code above raises an `AssertionError` like below.

```python
{0: {'A': 1, 'B': 'x'}, 1: {'A': 2, 'B': 'y'}}
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
<class 'dict'>
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[19], line 22
     18 print(type(out))
     19 print(type(out[0]))
     20 
     21 assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
---> 22 assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # fails

AssertionError:
```

This suggests `DataFrame.to_dict(..., into=...)` applying `into` only to the outer mapping when `orient="index"`.

In the example above, the outer returned object is `MyDict`, but each nested row mapping is a plain `dict`.

I checked whether this behavior is intended, but the docstrings of both functions
```python
pandas.core.frame.DataFrame.to_dict()
pandas.core.methods.to_dict.to_dict()
```

describe the result as `dict-like`, but do not clarify whether nested mappings should also respect `into`:
```
    Parameters
    ----------
    orient : str {'dict', 'list', 'series', 'split', 'tight', 'records', 'index'}
        Determines the type of the values of the dictionary.
    ...
    - 'index' : dict like {index -> {column -> value}}
```

I also inspected the `to_dict` implementation in `pandas.core.methods.to_dict`.
I believe this behavior comes from the following three return paths in the `elif orient == "index"` branch:
- plain dict is used directly:
```python
            return into_c(
                (t[0], dict(zip(df.columns, map(maybe_box_native, t[1:]), strict=True)))
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```
```python
            return into_c(
                (t[0], dict(zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)))
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```
- a dict comprehension is used directly, bypassing `into_c` for the nested mapping:
```python
            return into_c(
                (
                    t[0],
                    {
                        column: maybe_box_native(v)
                        if i in object_dtype_indices_as_set
                        else v
                        for i, (column, v) in enumerate(
                            zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)
                        )
                    },
                )
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```

This could be fixed by using the standardized mapping constructor `into_c` for the nested row mappings as well. For example, the dict-comprehension branch could be changed to:
```python
            return into_c(
                (
                    t[0],
                    into_c(
                        (
                            column,
                            maybe_box_native(v)
                            if i in object_dtype_indices_as_set
                            else v,
                        )
                        for i, (column, v) in enumerate(
                            zip(columns, t[1:], strict=True)
                        )
                    ),
                )
                for t in df.itertuples(name=None)
            )
```


With this change, the following code passes:
```python

class MyDict(dict):
    pass


df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "A": [1, 2],
        "B": ["x", "y"],
    }
)


out = to_dict(df, "index", into=MyDict)


print(out)
print(type(out))
print(type(out[0]))

assert isinstance(out, MyDict)
assert isinstance(out[0], MyDict)  # success
```

```
{0: {'A': 1, 'B': 'x'}, 1: {'A': 2, 'B': 'y'}}
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
<class '__main__.MyDict'>
```

I would be happy to open a pull request for this.

### Expected Behavior

Expected behavior:
```python
result = df.to_dict(orient="index", into=MyDict)

type(result)
# <class '__main__.MyDict'>

type(result[0])
# <class '__main__.MyDict'>
```

In other words, the result should be equivalent to:
```
MyDict(
    {
        0: MyDict({"A": 1, "B": "x"}),
        1: MyDict({"A": 2, "B": "y"}),
    }
)
```

title: BUG: assert_series_equal ignores check_series_type=False for ndarray subclass-backed Series on exact comparison path
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd 
import numpy as np

class OtherArray(np.ndarray):
    pass 

arr = np.array([1])

left = pd.Series(arr)
right = pd.Series(arr.view(OtherArray))

assert left.equals(right) 
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(left, right, check_series_type=False)
```

### Issue Description

`pd.testing.assert_series_equal` fails when comparing two equal `Series` objects if one is backed by a plain `np.ndarray` and the other is backed by an `np.ndarray` subclass, even when `check_series_type=False` is passed.

In the reproduction, you can observe that the two Series have the same dtype, values, index, and compare equal via `Series.equals`, but `assert_series_equal` still fails because it checks the concrete class of the internal backing arrays.

The error message is also misleading: it reports “Series classes are different”, but the classes shown are the backing array classes (`ndarray` vs `OtherArray`), not the `Series` classes.

 Full error:

```
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 13
     10 right = pd.Series(arr.view(OtherArray))
     12 assert left.equals(right) 
---> 13 pd.testing.assert_series_equal(left, right, check_series_type=False)

    [... skipping hidden 3 frame]

File <hidden_path>/lib/python3.13/site-packages/pandas/_testing/asserters.py:620, in raise_assert_detail(obj, message, left, right, diff, first_diff, index_values)
    617 if first_diff is not None:
    618     msg += f"\n{first_diff}"
--> 620 raise AssertionError(msg)

AssertionError: Series are different

Series classes are different
[left]:  ndarray
[right]: OtherArray
```

### Expected Behavior

The assertion should pass, since both objects are Series, their values are equal, their dtype is equal, and `check_series_type=False` indicates that concrete Series type differences should not be checked.

I suspect the right fix is for the `check_series_type` check to propogate into `assert_numpy_array_equal`
