title: BUG: Incoherent dynamic dtype changes in `.map()`
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Issue Description

In `a.map(b)`, when both a and b are Series and b's dtype is non-nullable, Pandas dynamically changes the output dtype if it can't match all the keys.

This behaviour changed in the nightlies vs. 3.0; however I am seeing inconsistencies which make little sense to me.

### Use case 1: Not all elements of `a.values` are in `b.index`
```python
a = pd.Series([1, 2])
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 3])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): np.float64

### Use case 2: Some values of `a` are NULL
```python
a = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="Int16")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): Float64

```python
a = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="int16[pyarrow]")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): double[pyarrow]

### Use case 3: All values of `a` are NULL
```python
a = pd.Series([None, None], dtype="Int16")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): Int16

```python
a = pd.Series([None, None], dtype="int16[pyarrow]")
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=[2, 1])
```
output (pandas 3.0): np.float64
output (pandas 3.1 nightly): double[pyarrow]


### Expected Behavior

IMHO there should be no difference in output in the three use cases.
Any of these output dtypes make sense to me:  

- `np.float64` (pandas 3.0 behaviour); on the principle that if `b.dtype` was a numpy dtype it should remain one even at the cost of loss of accuracy
- ` Int64`, or in other words the Pandas nullable equivalent of `b.dtype` (so Int8 if `b.dtype` is `np.int8`, etc.)
- `int64[pyarrow]`, or in other words the PyArrow nullable equivalent of `b.dtype`


### Installed Versions

pyarrow                           24.0.0 

vs.

pyarrow               25.0.0.dev70

title: API: how to handle time zone (DST) transitions in the distant future?
body:
Historically, by using `pytz` by default for time zones, tz-aware data had wrong offsets for DST periods after 2038 (e.g. see https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/33061 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/28207, and documented at https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/3.0/user_guide/timeseries.html#working-with-time-zones (scroll down to the 5th(!) warning box), sidenote: we should update this).

The same happens if you were using `dateutil.tz` time zones, and the short summary is that pytz and dateutil are only parsing the Version 1 TZif files, those don't include a "rule" for future times, and therefore typically include transitions times extrapolated to the future, but because of 32bit are limited to dates up to 2038.

This issue was fixed by switching to `zoneinfo` by default (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/34916) in pandas 3.0, since zoneinfo supports the newer versions of TZif files, and can use a rule-based logic for determining the offset for distant dates.

However, then after improving the performance for `zoneinfo` timezones to also use our internal fast binary search of the transition points (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64379) in pandas 3.0.3, this changed this behaviour again, because now we have to pre-populate our array of transition dates (to use for the binary search), and the linked PR decided to do that up to 2100 (meaning we only get correct offsets up to 2100, and not for later dates, see the example below).  
In https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65705, I am extending that cut-off from 2100 to 2262.

While having tz-aware data so far in the future is a bit a debatable use case, having an arbitrary cut off after which it behaves differently is not ideal.

Options:

- Decide we are OK with an arbitrary cut-off if it is far enough in the future (e.g. 2262) and document this
- Populate the transition data dynamically based on the range of the input data (eg by default fill up to year 2100, but if the input data max year is 2150, we recalculate it up to that date and update the cached data)
- Use our fast-path for a "normal" range (eg up to 2100) to cover most use cases, and then for dates after that, use the `zoneinfo` python API directly as a slower fallback


--

Code illustration:

```python
import pandas as pd

import dateutil.tz
import zoneinfo
import pytz

arr = pd.to_datetime([
    "2000-01-01", "2000-07-01",
    "2036-01-01", "2036-07-01",
    "2038-01-01", "2038-07-01",
    "2100-01-01", "2100-07-01",
    "2200-01-01", "2200-07-01"
], utc=True)
```

With pytz / default in pandas < 3:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert("Europe/Brussels"))   # pandas < 3
>>> print(arr.tz_convert(pytz.timezone("Europe/Brussels")))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 01:00:00+01:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[ns, Europe/Brussels]', freq=None)
```

With dateutil:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert(dateutil.tz.gettz("Europe/Brussels")))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 01:00:00+01:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 01:00:00+01:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[us, tzfile('/usr/share/zoneinfo/Europe/Brussels')]', freq=None)
```

With zoneinfo in pandas 2.3 or 3.0.0 - 3.0.2:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert("Europe/Brussels"))  # pandas >= 3.0
>>> print(arr.tz_convert(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("Europe/Brussels")))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 02:00:00+02:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]', freq=None)
```

With default zoneinfo in pandas 3.0.3:

```python
>>> print(arr.tz_convert("Europe/Brussels"))
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2000-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2036-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2036-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',
               '2038-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2038-07-01 02:00:00+02:00',  # 2038 is now correct, but 2100 and above not
               '2100-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2100-07-01 01:00:00+02:00',
               '2200-01-01 01:00:00+01:00', '2200-07-01 01:00:00+02:00'],
              dtype='datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]', freq=None)

```

title: ENH: Add `df.corrupt()` accessor to inject random faults and typos for Data Science education
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

In Data Science and AI education, teaching students how to clean and preprocess "dirty data" (handling missing values, detecting outliers, removing duplicates, and fixing text typos) is a critical skill. 

Currently, professors and students struggle to find realistic, messy datasets for practice. When using clean benchmark datasets (like Iris or Titanic), users have to write long, repetitive custom scripts from scratch just to artificially mess up the data for testing and educational purposes. There is no built-in, one-stop tool in Pandas to inject controlled chaos into a DataFrame.


### Feature Description

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import random
import string

@pd.api.extensions.register_dataframe_accessor("corrupt")
class CorruptAccessor:
    """
    A vectorized Pandas DataFrame accessor to inject synthetic anomalies, 
    missing values, outliers, duplicates, and smart human-like typos 
    for educational and pipeline testing purposes.
    """
    def __init__(self, pandas_obj):
        self._obj = pandas_obj

    def _resolve_count(self, param, total_elements):
        """Helper to support both exact integer counts and float percentages."""
        if isinstance(param, float) and 0.0 <= param <= 1.0:
            return int(param * total_elements)
        elif isinstance(param, (int, np.integer)):
            return int(param)
        else:
            raise TypeError("Parameters must be either an int (count) or a float between 0.0 and 1.0 (ratio).")

    def __call__(self, num_nan=0, num_outliers=0, num_duplicates=0, num_typos=0, random_state=None):
        if random_state is not None:
            np.random.seed(random_state)
            random.seed(random_state)

        # Work on a deep copy to guarantee immutability of the source dataset
        df = self._obj.copy()
        num_rows, num_cols = df.shape
        total_cells = num_rows * num_cols
        
        if num_rows == 0 or num_cols == 0:
            return df

        # --- 1. Resolve and Validate Injection Targets ---
        n_nan = self._resolve_count(num_nan, total_cells)
        if n_nan > total_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved NaNs ({n_nan}) cannot exceed total cells ({total_cells}).")

        numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
        total_numeric_cells = num_rows * len(numeric_cols)
        n_outliers = self._resolve_count(num_outliers, total_numeric_cells)
        if n_outliers > total_numeric_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved outliers ({n_outliers}) cannot exceed total numeric cells ({total_numeric_cells}).")

        n_duplicates = self._resolve_count(num_duplicates, num_rows)
        
        text_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns
        total_text_cells = num_rows * len(text_cols)
        n_typos = self._resolve_count(num_typos, total_text_cells)
        if n_typos > total_text_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved typos ({n_typos}) cannot exceed total text cells ({total_text_cells}).")

        # --- 2. Vectorized Fault Injection Pipelines ---

        # Pipeline A: Global Vectorized NaN Injection
        if n_nan > 0:
            flat_indices = np.random.choice(total_cells, size=n_nan, replace=False)
            nan_mask = np.zeros(total_cells, dtype=bool)
            nan_mask[flat_indices] = True
            nan_mask = nan_mask.reshape(num_rows, num_cols)
            
            for i, col in enumerate(df.columns):
                col_mask = nan_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    df.iloc[col_mask, i] = np.nan

        # Pipeline B: Statistically Robust Outlier Injection (Vectorized per Column)
        if n_outliers > 0 and len(numeric_cols) > 0:
            flat_num_indices = np.random.choice(total_numeric_cells, size=n_outliers, replace=False)
            outlier_mask = np.zeros(total_numeric_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(numeric_cols))
            outlier_mask.ravel()[flat_num_indices] = True
            
            for i, col in enumerate(numeric_cols):
                col_mask = outlier_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    std_dev = df[col].std()
                    if pd.isna(std_dev) or std_dev == 0:
                        std_dev = 1.0
                    df.loc[col_mask, col] = (df.loc[col_mask, col] * 3) + (5 * std_dev)

        # Pipeline C: Vectorized Duplicate Injection
        if n_duplicates > 0:
            duplicated_rows = df.sample(n=n_duplicates, replace=True, random_state=random_state)
            df = pd.concat([df, duplicated_rows], ignore_index=True)

        # Pipeline D: Smart Realistic Text Typo Injection
        if n_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0:
            flat_text_indices = np.random.choice(total_text_cells, size=n_typos, replace=False)
            typo_mask = np.zeros(total_text_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(text_cols))
            typo_mask.ravel()[flat_text_indices] = True
            
            def _mutate_string(val):
                """Helper to simulate realistic human typing errors dynamically."""
                s = str(val)
                if not s or s == "nan":
                    return s
                
                # Randomly pick an error type: deletion, substitution, or insertion
                operation = random.choice(['delete', 'substitute', 'insert'])
                random_char = random.choice(string.ascii_lowercase)
                
                if len(s) <= 1:
                    return s + random_char
                
                if operation == 'delete':
                    return s[:-1]
                elif operation == 'substitute':
                    return s[:-1] + random_char
                else:  # insert
                    return s + random_char

            for i, col in enumerate(text_cols):
                col_mask = typo_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    # Apply the dynamic typo mutation function strictly to the masked cells
                    df.loc[col_mask, col] = df.loc[col_mask, col].apply(_mutate_string)

        return df



### Alternative Solutions

### Current Workaround / Alternative Code:

Currently, users and educators have to write verbose, loop-heavy, or non-vectorized custom functions to perturb their data cell-by-cell. A typical suboptimal workaround looks like this:

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import random

def manual_corrupt(df, num_nan=0, num_typos=0):
    df_dirty = df.copy()
    
    # 1. Non-vectorized manual loop for NaNs
    if num_nan > 0:
        for _ in range(num_nan):
            r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1)
            c = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[1] - 1)
            df_dirty.iat[r, c] = np.nan
            
    # 2. Slow cell-by-cell scalar string manipulation for typos
    text_cols = df_dirty.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns
    if num_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0:
        for _ in range(num_typos):
            r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1)
            col = random.choice(text_cols)
            current_val = str(df_dirty.at[r, col])
            # Naive typo injection (just drops the last character)
            if len(current_val) > 1:
                df_dirty.at[r, col] = current_val[:-1]
                
    return df_dirty


### Additional Context

This feature would significantly benefit the Data Science, Machine Learning, and AI educational ecosystem (such as university courses, bootcamps, and online interactive notebooks). 

Teaching "Data Cleaning" is notoriously hard without messy data, and creating realistic "dirty data" natively with one simple, reproducible function call (`df.corrupt(...)`) would seamlessly close the gap between pristine benchmark datasets and real-world preprocessing challenges. 

I am willing to contribute or iterate on this implementation based on core-dev feedback regarding where this best fits into the Pandas codebase.

title: ENH/API: Architectural Audit - Are other inplace=True methods bypassing CoW reference tracking?
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

### Background
While investigating a memory corruption issue yesterday (reported in #65664  and patched in PR #65675 ), I found a structural vulnerability in how the computation engine interacts with Pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write (CoW) architecture. 

Specifically, `df.eval("new=old", inplace=True)` was bypassing CoW protections. The `eval` engine reached into the `BlockManager`, extracted the raw data arrays, evaluated them, and handed them back. Because the data took a detour through the external computation engine, the CoW reference tracking metadata was stripped. The DataFrame assumed the returned array was unshared memory, leading to silent memory corruption when the alias was later modified.

### The Architectural Question
My patch forces an explicit `.copy()` before assignment if `inplace=True` inside `pandas.core.computation.eval`. However, this raises a much larger architectural question: **Are there other C-engine, Cython, or NumExpr-routed methods that are secretly leaking CoW tracking data when `inplace=True` is invoked?**

### Proposed Audit Targets
We know that standard `__setitem__` handles CoW perfectly. But any method that extracts raw arrays, computes externally, and attempts to write back `inplace` is at risk. I propose a systematic audit of the following `inplace=True` methods to ensure they aren't making the same tracking error:

1. **`DataFrame.query(inplace=True)`:** Since this relies on the exact same underlying `pandas.core.computation` engines (`numexpr` / `python`) as `eval`, it is the most likely candidate for a parallel vulnerability.
2. **`DataFrame.where()` & `DataFrame.mask()`:** When backed by external engines or fast-path Cython blocks.
3. **`DataFrame.fillna()` & `DataFrame.replace()`:** Specifically when operating on mixed dtypes that might force a block consolidation or split during the inplace write.
4. **`DataFrame.clip()`**

### Action Items
Rather than playing whack-a-mole with memory bugs, I suggest we:
1. Identify all `inplace=True` paths that route through `numexpr` or bypass the standard `NDFrame.__setitem__` API.
2. Implement a standardized CoW "alias corruption" test suite specifically targeting these external engine routes.
3. Determine if we need a centralized validation wrapper that explicitly checks reference counts when C-engines return data for inplace assignment.

I am happy to lead the audit on `.query()` and `.where()` to start, but wanted to bring this to the core team's attention to see if there is already a broader strategy for validating `inplace` safety under CoW. Thoughts?

### Feature Description

I propose implementing a two-phase solution to secure the CoW perimeter:

**1. A Centralized Testing Utility:**
Introduce a new test utility in `pandas/tests/copy_view/` specifically designed to test external-engine mutations. 
Pseudocode:
```python
def assert_cow_inplace_safe(df, operation_func):
    """
    Ensures that an inplace operation does not corrupt aliases 
    if it routes through an external engine.
    """
    df_copy = df.copy()
    alias = df["column_name"]
    
    # Perform inplace operation that might strip CoW tracking
    operation_func(df) 
    
    # Mutate the alias
    alias.iloc[0] = modified_value
    
    # If the original dataframe was mutated, the CoW perimeter failed.
    assert_frame_equal(df, df_copy) 
```

.........
2. A C-Engine Return Wrapper:
If the audit finds multiple leaks in .query(), .where(), etc., rather than patching them individually, we should implement a validation layer inside BlockManager.setitem_inplace (or the equivalent API) that explicitly asserts: if pd.options.mode.copy_on_write: assert result.refs is safe before mapping the C-engine memory back to the dataframe.



### **Alternative Solutions**
**Alternative 1: The "Whack-a-Mole" Approach (Status Quo)**
We do nothing structurally, and wait for users to report data corruption bugs one by one as they upgrade to Pandas 3.0. This risks user trust in the new CoW architecture.

**Alternative 2: Do nothing and wait for PDEP-8**
Since `inplace=True` is broadly slated for deprecation and removal in Pandas 4.0 (PDEP-8), we could argue that investing in `inplace` infrastructure isn't worth the time. *However*, because users will be relying on Pandas 3.x during the CoW transition period, allowing silent data corruption to exist during this window is highly dangerous. We need to secure the perimeter until `inplace` is officially removed.

### Additional Context

This architectural concern was triggered by my investigation into Issue #65664, where I successfully patched a live CoW tracking bypass in `DataFrame.eval(inplace=True)` via PR #65675.

title: BUG: Data corruption after `.eval(..., inplace=True)`.
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
nums = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=10_000).astype(np.int32)
df = pd.DataFrame({"nums": nums.copy()})
df.eval("nums2 = nums", inplace=True)
mask = rng.random(10_000) > 0.5
df.loc[mask, "nums2"] = 0
assert np.array_equal(df["nums"].to_numpy(), nums), "BUG: nums was corrupted!"
```

### Issue Description

When using `df.eval("new=old",inplace=True)` to initialize a column with another column, no genuine copy is made, leading to data corruption when modifying column entries through `df.loc`. This affects pandas starting from 3.0.0 up to the latest version 3.0.3.

### Expected Behavior

Assert should pass. Pandas should always create a data copy when initializing with `df.eval("new=old", inplace=True)`. Writes to the new column through `df.loc[]` should not affect the source column.

title: BUG: DataFrame.melt silently corrupts data on var_name output-name collisions
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "a": [10, 20], "b": [100, 200]})
# var_name collides with the id_vars column "id"
out = df.melt(id_vars="id", var_name="id")
print(out)

output :
 
    id id  value
  0  a  a     10
  1  a  a     20
  2  b  b    100
  3  b  b    200
```

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.melt` can silently overwrite `id_vars` data with variable labels when the resolved `var_name` output column collides with an `id_var` name. Related output-name collisions, such as `var_name` colliding with `value_name` or duplicate entries in a list-like `var_name`, can also produce silently incorrect output. pandas already rejects `value_name` collisions with existing column labels, but analogous output-name validation is missing for `var_name`

### Expected Behavior

melt should raise a ValueError because the requested output column names would be duplicated:

["id", "id", "value"]

The original id_vars data should not be silently overwritten.

title: PERF: pandas.io.sql.has_table slow for ADBC driver with large database
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

We actually noticed the slowness from `pandas.read_sql`, but narrowed the problem down to its call to `has_table`. We're calling `read_sql` with a query so it will always be a miss for `has_table`.

```python
import time
import pandas.io.sql as pd_sql
from adbc_driver_snowflake.dbapi import connect

with connect("<database URI>") as conn:  # Connection to a large database
    start = time.perf_counter()
    pd_sql.has_table("foo", conn)  # Where foo does not match a table
    end = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"Took {end - start} seconds")
```

The problem sees to be in [`pandas.io.sql.ADBCDatabase.has_table`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/sql.py#L2429-L2431), which calls [`self.con.adbc_get_objects()`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/python/api/adbc_driver_manager.html#adbc_driver_manager.dbapi.Connection.adbc_get_objects) without passing `depth=`. The default depth is `"all"`, which enumerates objects down to the columns. Adding `depth="tables"` speeds things up dramatically for us—from 53 seconds without `depth="tables"` down to 3 seconds with.

body:
### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {'a': range(3), 'b': range(10, 13), 'c': range(3)}
).rename(columns={'b': 'a'})

print(df)
print(df.eval('a == 1'))
print(pd.eval('a == 1', resolvers=(df,)))
```

### Issue Description

`Dataframe.eval ` behaves differently from `pandas.eval()` when a `DataFrame` contains duplicated column names.

In the example above, the `DataFrame` has two columns named `a`. Evaluating the expression `a == 1` appears to only evaluate one of the duplicated columns (the second one in this case), and returning a `pandas.Series`

In contrast, `pd.eval( ... )` evaluates both duplicated columns and returns a `DataFrame`. 

Similar to #59950

### Expected Behavior

It would be helpful to clarify whether duplicated column names are intended to be supported in both APIs. 

Possible expected behaviors could include: 
* both methods behaving similarly
* raising an explicit exception when expressions reference duplicated names

title: ENH: Improve missing column KeyError message in DataFrame access
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

# Problem Description
Currently, when users attempt to access a column that does not exist in a DataFrame using:

df["Age"]

Pandas raises a generic error message:

KeyError: 'Age'

While technically correct, this message provides very limited context for users, especially beginners.

The current behavior does not:

explain why the error occurred,
show available columns,
help users identify possible typos,
improve debugging experience.

This can make debugging slower and more frustrating for new users working with DataFrames.

Example Reproduction
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Pradip", "Rahul"]
})

print(df["Age"])

Current output:

KeyError: 'Age'

# Expected Behavior

The error message should provide more contextual information.

Possible improved output:

KeyError: Column 'Age' not found in DataFrame.
Available columns: ['Name']

OR:

KeyError: Column 'Age' does not exist.
Did you mean: 'Name'?

### Feature Description

# Feature Description

Enhance the DataFrame column-access error handling mechanism to produce more descriptive and user-friendly error messages when a requested column is missing.

Potential improvements include:

  1.displaying available column names,
  2.suggesting similar column names,
  3.clarifying that the requested column does not exist,
  4.improving beginner usability.

This enhancement would improve:

  debugging experience,
  developer productivity,
  accessibility for new Pandas users.

### Alternative Solutions

# Proposed Solution

Locate the internal column access logic (likely in:

pandas/core/frame.py

)

and replace the generic:

raise KeyError(key)

with a more informative exception message.

Example:

raise KeyError(
    f"Column '{key}' not found in DataFrame. "
    f"Available columns: {list(self.columns)}"
)

### Additional Context

# Additional Context

Large DataFrames

Listing all columns may create excessively long error messages for wide DataFrames.

Possible mitigation:

truncate displayed column list,
show only first few columns.

Example:

  Available columns: ['Name', 'Marks', 'Email', ...]

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

a = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3, 4], mask=[False, True, False, True])

# BUG: mask is ignored completely
pd.array(a)
# Output:
# <IntegerArray>
# [1, 2, 3, 4]
# Length: 4, dtype: Int64

# For comparison, pd.Series handles the mask but changes dtype to float
pd.Series(a)
# Output:
# 0 1.0
# 1 NaN
# 2 3.0
# 3 NaN
# dtype: float64
```

### Issue Description

NumPy [masked arrays](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/maskedarray.generic.html#what-is-a-masked-array) are used to define arrays with missing values, similar to pandas extension arrays. However, converting to `pd.array` currently ignores the mask completely and masked values appear as regular values.

Converting to `pd.Series` does respect the missing values, but the dtype is converted to `float` and the original dtype is not preserved in all cases.

This behavior is inconsistent with user expectations and with how `pd.Series` handles masked arrays.

The same issue occurs with string masked arrays where the mask is also ignored by `pd.array`.

### Expected Behavior

Masked values should be converted to pd.NA and the appropriate nullable dtype should be preserved, such as Int64 or string, instead of ignoring the mask or coercing to float.

>>> pd.array(a)
<IntegerArray>
[1, <NA>, 3, <NA>]
Length: 4, dtype: Int64

title: BUG: pandas.DataFrame.max fails on datetime64[ns, ...] columns with different time zones and NaT in the data
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ONE_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Budapest")
OTHER_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Moscow")

# Example (works): different timezones, no NaT
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, OTHER_TZ]})
df1.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (works): same timezone, with NaT
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[ONE_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df2.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (fails): different timezone, with NaT
df3 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df3.max(axis=1) # Fails, as soon as we have a NaT
```

### Issue Description

In dataframes with datetime64 columns, max() fails with a `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'` when 2 different timezones and NaT values are both present. As long as we have 1 timezone or no NaTs, everything works as expected. The default behavior of max() is skipping nans, and NaT is interpreted as such correctly with the same timezone. Once the timezone is different, it is treated as a float and the comparison fails.

It seems like during the max() operation, since timezones differ, rows are coerced into an `object` dtype. The NaT is leaking into the underlying numpy amax as a float instead of being safely skipped or masked out before the comparison occurs.

### Expected Behavior

Truly skipping NaTs as a default in max() before attempting the comparison of the remaining datetime64 values.

title: DOC: Missing docstring for enable_data_resource_formatter in printing module
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

pandas/io/formats/printing.py

### Documentation problem

The function `enable_data_resource_formatter` in `pandas/io/formats/printing.py` does not have a docstring describing its purpose or behavior. 

This function performs non-trivial logic, including:
- Detecting whether the code is running in an IPython environment
- Dynamically registering a formatter for the `application/vnd.dataresource+json` mimetype
- Enabling or disabling that  formatter based on the 'enable' parameter

Without documentation, it is unclear:
- What this formatter is used for
- When this function should be called

This makes the function difficult to understand and maintain for contributors. 

### Suggested fix for documentation

The current implementation currently has no docstring, so developers must read and interpret the source code to understand its purpose and behavior.

Adding a docstring would improve the documentation by:
- Clearly explaining the purpose of the function 
- Describing the meaning of the `enable` parameter

This makes the function easier to understand, reduces the likelihood of misuse, and improves maintainability for contributors.

title: BUG: `Series.values` returns inconsistent type (`ndarray` vs `MaskedArray`) depending on whether DataFrame rows are pre-sorted by groupby key
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

print(pd.__version__)

bins = np.linspace(0., 100., 101)
xc   = 0.5 * (bins[1:] + bins[:-1])

for label, x, y in [
    ("non-empty, y sorted by bin",   np.ma.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]), np.array([25., 50., 75.])),
    ("non-empty, y unsorted by bin", np.ma.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]), np.array([50., 75., 25.])),
    ("empty",                        np.ma.array([], dtype=float),  np.array([])),
]:
    df = pd.DataFrame()
    df["x"] = x
    df["y"] = y
    df = df.loc[:, ["x", "y"]]
    df.reset_index(inplace=True)
    df["bin"] = pd.cut(df["y"].values, bins=bins, labels=[str(c) for c in xc])
    for name, grp in df.groupby("bin", observed=False):
        print(f"{label}: {type(grp['x'].values).__name__}")
        break
```
prints
```
3.1.0.dev0+824.gb00d4f6710
non-empty, y sorted by bin: MaskedArray
non-empty, y unsorted by bin: ndarray
empty: MaskedArray
```

### Issue Description

When a `numpy.ma.MaskedArray` column is stored in a DataFrame and groups are iterated via `groupby(..., observed=False)`, the type returned by `Series.values` depends on whether the rows happen to be pre-sorted by the groupby key and on whether the DataFrame is empty. The same column, same dtype, same group, just different row ordering or DataFrame size, produces either `ndarray` or `MaskedArray`.

### Expected Behavior

`Series.values` should return a consistent type regardless of whether the underlying DataFrame rows are sorted, unsorted, or empty. Given the column dtype is numeric (e.g. `float64`), `ndarray` is the expected return type in all three cases.

title: API: tracker for single-element listlike RHS inconsistency in setitem
body:
`obj[key] = [42]` (or `np.array([42])`) does different things depending on the accessor, the key shape, the dtype, and the block structure of unrelated columns:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [10, 20, 30], "y": [40, 50, 60]},
                  index=["a", "b", "c"]).astype(object)

# list RHS
df.loc["a", "x"]      = [42]            # cell stores [42]
df.loc["a", ["x"]]    = [42]            # cell stores 42
df.loc[["a"], ["x"]]  = [42]            # cell stores 42
df.iloc[0, 0]         = [42]            # cell stores [42]
df.iloc[0, [0]]       = [42]            # cell stores 42
df.at["a", "x"]       = [42]            # cell stores [42]

# np.array RHS — yet another set of outcomes
df.loc["a", "x"]      = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42)   (0-D!)
df.loc["a", ["x"]]    = np.array([42])  # cell stores np.int64(42)
df.loc[["a"], ["x"]]  = np.array([42])  # cell stores 42
df.iloc[0, 0]         = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42)
df.iloc[0, [0]]       = np.array([42])  # cell stores np.int64(42)
df.at["a", "x"]       = np.array([42])  # cell stores array(42)
```

Six open issues describe pieces of this directly. Filing as a single umbrella so they can be considered together.

## Bull's-eye open issues

**#16864 (2017) — One item lists are assigned into dataframes as single items.** `df.loc[[0,1], 'new_col'] = [['one_item'], ['one_item']]` stores `'one_item'` (the inner string) in each row instead of `['one_item']` (the list). The reporter wanted to populate a list-valued column row-by-row and was surprised that single-element nested lists got unwrapped while multi-element ones didn't.

**#25806 (2019) — Effect of assigning list to DataFrame cell depends on unrelated column's type.** `df.loc['a', 'foo'] = ['123']` stores `['123']` on a fresh DataFrame, but the *same* assignment on the same DataFrame stores `'123'` once an unrelated column has been cast to float. Behavior depends on the block layout, not on user intent. Same example shows `.at` and `.loc` diverging on the same input.

**#30649 (2019) — `df.at[...] = ['some list']` doesn't set object dtype on column creation.** Setting a list via `.at` to a non-existent column creates the column with the wrong dtype; the first row stores the unwrapped scalar `'a'` while subsequent rows (after the column exists) correctly store `['a']`. Same accessor, same RHS, two different outcomes depending on whether the column already exists.

**#35006 (2020) — Different behavior when setting a list(scalar) to entire column vs filtered rows.** `df["new"] = list_of_arrays` produces one outcome; `df.loc[mask, "new"] = list_of_arrays` produces another, even when the mask matches every row. Multi-step repro showing four "expected" cases and two "unexpected" ones with the same RHS construction.

**#53565 (2023, regression from 2.0) — Reassigning a Series index with a 1-D length-1 ndarray loses dimension.** First `s['whatever'] = np.array([1])` stores shape `(1,)` as expected. *Second* assignment of the same value collapses to shape `()`. Reproducible 1.5 → 2.0 regression, no movement since.

**#57923 (2024) — Inconsistent implicit conversion of 1-arrays inside DataFrames.** `df.at[0, 0] = np.arange(2)` stores `array([0, 1])`; `df.at[1, 0] = np.arange(1)` stores `np.int64(0)`. Length-1 ndarrays get silently unwrapped to scalars where length-2+ ndarrays don't, on the same accessor with the same dtype. Reporter notes pandas can be tricked into holding 1-arrays via `applymap`, demonstrating the unwrap is at the setitem boundary and not a storage limitation.

## Closely related — broader setitem consistency

- **#26333 (2019)** — REGR: assigning a tuple/scalar-with-length to an object-dtype cell stopped working in 0.23, "Must have equal len keys and value when setting with an iterable".
- **#46544 (2022)** — `DataFrame.loc` and `DataFrame.__setitem__` give different results for the same 2-D ndarray RHS.
- **#57962 (2024)** — `df.loc[1, 2] = np.zeros(3)` into an object-dtype cell raises despite the dtype permitting it (1.4 → 2.x regression).
- **#61223 (2025)** — `.at` setting an iterable fails when the column doesn't yet exist, succeeds afterwards.
- **#15490 (2017)** — `.at` / `.loc` modifies the DataFrame even when the assignment raises.
- **#45769 (2022)** — MultiIndex `loc` with an n×2 list assignment fails despite shape match.
- **#62369 (2025)** — API question on what dtype setitem-with-expansion should infer.

## Umbrella / meta

- **#55935 (2023)** — PDEP-6: setitem casting (the standing umbrella for setitem semantic decisions).
- **#27911 (2019)** — API: when to cast list-like to ndarray, check len match (the arithmetic-side analog of this question).
- **#60218 (2024)** — ERR: consistent error messages for unsupported setitem values.

## Adjacent — same family, peripheral

- **#42549 (2021)** — list-like objects broadcast to each row (1.3 regression caused by `is_list_like` not detecting some sequences).
- **#46974 (2022)** — DataFrame setitem with DataFrame RHS doesn't align column names.
- **#51386 (2023)** — `Series.__setitem__` with Series value: alignment vs replacement question.
- **#53996 (2023)** — DOC: is the behavior of setitem with repeated keys defined?
- **#57765 (2024)** — Setting a 2-D numpy array as a column uses only the first column.
- **#61026 (2025)** — Setting column with 2-D object-dtype array raises.

Original-intent context for the carve-outs that any fix would need to revisit: **#19474** (the explicit unwrap-on-listlike-LHS), **#37629** (nested-container preservation), **#44103** (force-split-path for scalar-row + listlike-col).

## Why one tracker

These six bull's-eye issues are not separate bugs in separate corners — they're the same inconsistency surfacing at six different accessor / dtype / shape / expansion-vs-existing combinations, on a code path that has accumulated independent decision points at multiple layers. Discussing them in one place makes the matrix visible and lets any fix (or deprecation) be evaluated against all six at once rather than one at a time.

title: BUG: Index.get_indexer matches pd.NA against NaN for list input but not ndarray input
body:
`Index.get_indexer` gives different answers for `[pd.NA]` (list) vs `np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)` on a NaN-containing index. The list path normalizes `pd.NA` to NaN; the ndarray path doesn't. `Index.get_loc` (scalar lookup) also matches. This propagates into `Index.drop`, which routes through `com.index_labels_to_array` (producing an ndarray) and so cannot drop a NaN-labeled entry given `pd.NA`.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.Index([np.nan, "b"])

idx.get_loc(np.nan)                              # 0
idx.get_loc(pd.NA)                               # 0  <- matches

idx.get_indexer([pd.NA])                         # array([0])   <- matches
idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)) # array([-1])  <- doesn't
idx.get_indexer(pd.Index([pd.NA]))               # array([-1])  <- doesn't

idx.drop([pd.NA])   # KeyError: '[<NA>] not found in axis'
idx.drop([np.nan])  # works
```

Surfaces from `merge`: a DataFrame built with `{pd.NA: ...}` has columns coerced to a NaN label, so `merge(left_on=pd.NA, right_on=pd.NA)` resolves keys correctly via `_get_label_or_level_values` (which uses `get_loc`) but fails on the `right_drop` path via `_drop_labels_or_levels` -> `Index.drop`.

The scalar-lookup paths (`get_loc`, list `get_indexer`) treat `pd.NA` as matching NaN; the array-lookup paths (ndarray/Index `get_indexer`, `Index.drop`) don't. Either both should match, or neither should.

title: PERF: skip redundant Index.equals calls in pd.concat
body:
### Problem

`pd.concat` compares the same logical pair of indexes twice:

1. `union_indexes` → `all_indexes_same` (`indexes/api.py:337`) walks the inputs pairwise (`first.equals(idx)` for each other), and returns `indexes[0]` when they all match.
2. Then `_get_result` (`reshape/concat.py:652`) re-runs `new_labels.equals(obj_labels)` per obj to decide whether reindexing is needed — re-asking the same question.

In the common case where input frames are separately-constructed with content-equal-but-identity-distinct column indexes, ~50% of all `Index.equals` calls under `pd.concat` are this duplicate.

### Numbers (per call, inputs pre-built outside the timer)

| workload | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 0.62 ms | 0.50 ms | **1.25x** |
| 1000 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 6.76 ms | 5.70 ms | 1.19x |
| 100 frames, 20 cols, multi-block (dict-built) | 0.64 ms | 0.49 ms | **1.31x** |
| 20 sibling-tables, axis=1, 1000 rows | 0.19 ms | 0.15 ms | 1.25x |
| 200 frames built fresh + concat (read-many-files) | 7.96 ms | 7.58 ms | 1.05x |

"After" estimated by short-circuiting duplicate `(id(self), id(other))` pairs with a per-concat memoization cache.

### Beneficiary

Patterns that build frames separately then concat them: `pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f) for f in files])` and equivalents.

`groupby.apply` and `pd.concat([df.iloc[a:b] for ...])` see **zero** `Index.equals` calls (slices share the parent's Index identity, `_get_distinct_objs` collapses them) — this change is a no-op for those.

### Proposed change

Return an `all_equal` flag from `union_indexes` when it takes the `all_indexes_same`-True branch, and thread it through `_get_combined_index` → `new_axes` → `_get_result`. When True, `_get_result` skips the per-obj `equals` and uses empty indexers.

Happy to put up a PR.

title: PERF: cache BlockManager.get_dtypes() result
body:
### Problem

`BaseBlockManager.get_dtypes()` (`pandas/core/internals/managers.py:339`) rebuilds an object array on every call:

```python
def get_dtypes(self) -> npt.NDArray[np.object_]:
    dtypes = np.array([blk.dtype for blk in self.blocks], dtype=object)
    return dtypes.take(self.blknos)
```

It's called from a number of hot paths — `df.dtypes`, `DataFrame.fillna` (`generic.py:6391`), `select_dtypes`/`_get_numeric_data`, `DataFrame.apply` (`frame.py:15751`), `unique_dtypes` in repr/info (`generic.py:7136`), and twice per `iloc` setitem (`indexing.py:944, 975`). For wide, fragmented managers each call is O(nblocks) Python iteration plus an object-array allocation.

### Numbers (1000-col DataFrame, 335 blocks, mixed f8/i8/object)

| call | current | with cache | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mgr.get_dtypes()` | 47 us | 0.08 us | **608x** |
| `df.dtypes` | 58 us | 8.7 us | **6.7x** |

Caching saves the full cost on cache hits; `df.dtypes` retains ~8 us of unavoidable Series-construction overhead.

### Proposed change

Add a `_dtypes_cache` attribute on the manager, populated lazily in `get_dtypes()` and invalidated alongside the existing `_blknos` / `_interleaved_dtype` cache hooks (`managers.py:1411, 1497` and other block-mutation sites). The same invalidation pattern is already in place — adding one more entry is mechanical.

### Caveats

- The cached array must not be mutated in place by callers. A quick audit of callers shows they only read it (equality checks, `.take`, iteration) — no in-place writes — but worth confirming during review.
- `SingleBlockManager` already has only one block; the cache is still cheap and consistent.

Happy to put up a PR.

title: PERF: Replace dateutil-based parser fallback with a regex-based parser in tslibs.parsing
body:
In non-ISO8601 cases we use dateutil's parser, but this is 1) not-optimized pure-python and 2) parses some strings that we probably should raise on, e.g.:

"Jan"
"10am"
"5th"
"1234"

The hard part here is deciding exactly what cases we want to allow and a deprecation cycle for cases that we disallow.

Using a regex with a fixed set of formats would be significantly faster (preliminary benchmarks are 5-15x on cases with month name sand 100x on cases with "AM" or "PM").

Running list of issues that this might address: #17265

title: PERF: skip to_datetime cache=True overhead for input shapes where it cannot help
body:
#### Summary

`to_datetime(..., cache=True)` (the default) unconditionally runs the
`_maybe_cache` machinery — `Series(dtype=object)` construction +
`should_cache` which iterates up to 500 elements of the input — even on
inputs where `_convert_listlike_datetimes` is going to dispatch to a
non-parsing path or a path where caching has been measured to never help.
On these inputs `cache=True` is strictly slower than `cache=False`, by
margins ranging from a few percent to **~520×** at the worst.

All five "no-help" conditions are identifiable in O(1) time, before any
sampling, just by looking at `arg.dtype`, the `unit` kwarg, and the
`format` kwarg.

#### Affected input shapes (all O(1) to detect)

1. `unit is not None` — input is dispatched to `_to_datetime_with_unit`,
   which is a vectorized cast; caching cannot help.
2. `arg.dtype` is `np.dtype("M8[*]")` — already datetime64; `_convert_listlike_datetimes` short-circuits.
3. `arg.dtype` is `DatetimeTZDtype` — already tz-aware; short-circuits.
4. `arg.dtype` is `ArrowDtype` with `type is Timestamp` — short-circuits.
5. `format is not None and format != "mixed"` — `array_strptime` is fast
   enough that `pd.unique()` + `Series.map()` costs as much as just
   re-parsing; `cache=True` is never a measurable win on this path.

#### Reproducer

```python
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def best(fn, k=5):
    fn()  # warmup
    times = []
    for _ in range(k):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return min(times)


def bench(label, arg, **kwargs):
    t_off = best(lambda: pd.to_datetime(arg, cache=False, **kwargs))
    t_on = best(lambda: pd.to_datetime(arg, cache=True, **kwargs))
    print(f"{label:<35s}  off={t_off*1000:7.2f}ms  on={t_on*1000:7.2f}ms  on/off={t_on/t_off:.2f}x")


n = 100_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

arr_unit = np.arange(n, dtype="int64")
arr_dt64 = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=n, freq="s").to_numpy()
idx_tz = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=n, freq="s", tz="US/Eastern")
base_iso = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=100, freq="s").strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S").to_numpy()
arr_iso = base_iso[rng.integers(0, 100, n)]

bench("unit='s' int", arr_unit, unit="s")
bench("datetime64 ndarray", arr_dt64)
bench("DatetimeIndex tz=US/Eastern", idx_tz)
bench("ISO strings, format=...", arr_iso, format="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
```

#### Measurements

On `main` (today, n=100k unless noted):

| Input | `cache=False` | `cache=True` | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unit='s'` int (10% unique) | 0.07 ms | 0.78 ms | **11.0×** slower |
| `unit='s'` int (n=100k all-unique) | 0.07 ms | 0.92 ms | **13.4×** slower |
| `datetime64[ns]` ndarray | 0.03 ms | 0.07 ms | 2.6× slower |
| `DatetimeIndex` w/ tz (any n) | 0.01 ms | 6.15 ms | **~520×** slower |
| `ArrowDtype` timestamp (any n) | 0.01 ms | 0.64 ms | ~50× slower |
| ISO + explicit format (n=10k, 100 unique) | 0.82 ms | 1.19 ms | 1.45× slower |
| ISO + explicit format (n=10k, 10 unique) | 0.80 ms | 1.26 ms | 1.57× slower |

The DatetimeTZ case is the worst: `should_cache` does
`set(islice(arg, 500))`, which on a tz-aware DatetimeIndex materializes
500 `Timestamp` Python objects (~6 ms), and that cost is paid regardless
of `n`. A `to_datetime` round-trip on an already-converted `DatetimeIndex`
of any size is dominated entirely by this useless sampling step.

#### Where the caching gate lives

`pandas/core/tools/datetimes.py`:

- `_maybe_cache` is called from the dispatch in `to_datetime` (lines ~1081, 1090, 1104) **before** `_convert_listlike_datetimes` runs its dtype short-circuits (lines ~367–412).
- `should_cache` (lines 156–213) does the iteration that costs ~6 ms on tz-aware DTIs.

#### Proposed fix

Add an O(1) early-bail at the top of `_maybe_cache`:

```python
if cache:
    if unit is not None:
        return cache_array
    arg_dtype = getattr(arg, "dtype", None)
    if (
        lib.is_np_dtype(arg_dtype, "M")
        or isinstance(arg_dtype, DatetimeTZDtype)
        or (isinstance(arg_dtype, ArrowDtype) and arg_dtype.type is Timestamp)
    ):
        return cache_array
    if format is not None and format != "mixed":
        return cache_array
    ...
```

`unit` would need to be threaded from the dispatch sites (currently bound
in the partial only). No behavior change — every one of these inputs hits
a short-circuit / non-parsing path in the next call.

#### Out of scope (separate follow-ups)

- `format=None` on ISO strings where format inference succeeds → strptime path. Same loss profile as the explicit-format case, but only detectable by deferring the cache decision past format inference.
- `should_cache`'s `unique_share=0.7` threshold is calibrated for the slow
  dateutil path and is too generous for fast-parse inputs that get past
  the O(1) gate.

#### Pandas version
pandas `main` @ `501e319b0b`.

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.to_numeric.html

> **Returns:**
> **ret**
> Numeric if parsing succeeded. Return type depends on input. Series if Series, otherwise ndarray.

### Documentation problem

The documentation is missing these return types:

### Index

1-d specifically

Example:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.Index(['0']))
Index([0], dtype='int64')
```

Source:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L318-L323

### Scalars

Example:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric('0')
np.int64(0)
```

Source:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L202-L210

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L324-L325

### Additionally

"Numeric if parsing succeeded" implies there's a different return type if parsing failed, but the function would actually **raise** in that case (instead of returning), if I understand correctly. Or it would return NaN, but that's still a numeric type, even though it's called "not a number".

Also, the `dtype_backend` parameter says: "Back-end data type applied to the resultant **DataFrame**", but `to_numeric` can't return a DataFrame as far as I know. I tried it just to confirm:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]))
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series

>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]), dtype_backend='pyarrow')
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series

>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]), dtype_backend='numpy_nullable')
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series
```

### Suggested fix for documentation

I don't understand all the ins and outs of the function, but I'll try my best:

Change "Returns" to:
> **Returns:**
> **numeric**
> Return type depends on input. For numeric inputs, the type is preserved. For scalars: `int` if possible, otherwise `float`. For 1-d: Series if Series, Index if Index, otherwise ndarray.

Change `dtype_backend` paramter to: "Back-end data type applied to the resultant Series or Index"

title: API/BUG: .loc tuple ambiguity with MultiIndex when nlevels == ndim
body:
I [the human] asked Claude to post the following:

## Summary

When a DataFrame has a MultiIndex with `nlevels == ndim` (the most common case: a 2-level MI on a 2D DataFrame), tuple keys passed to `.loc` are fundamentally ambiguous between two interpretations:

1. **MI row key**: `df.loc[(a, b)]` means "the row with MultiIndex key `(a, b)`"
2. **Multi-axis indexing**: `df.loc[a, b]` means "row `a`, column `b`"

Python produces the same tuple `(a, b)` for both spellings. The current code resolves this ambiguity differently depending on context — getitem vs setitem, existing vs missing key, scalar vs slice — leading to a cluster of related bugs where the same syntax silently produces different results.

## Related issues

### Primary — same root ambiguity

| Issue | Status | Problem |
|-------|--------|---------|
| #14969 | Open | `df.loc[0, 0]` returns a DataFrame or a Series depending on the dtype of the inner MI level — identical syntax, different interpretation |
| #16396 | Open | `df.loc[1, 2]` uses the MI interpretation, but `df.loc[:1, 2]` and `df.loc[:, 2]` switch to multi-axis (column `2`) — incoherent |
| #27248 | Open | `df.loc[(1, 2019)] = [3, 4]` fails on setitem-with-expansion because the MI key `(1, 2019)` is misinterpreted as `(row=1, col=2019)` |
| #42603 | Open | `df.loc["foo", 0]` silently returns different things depending on whether `0` exists in MI level 1 — proposes an ambiguity error |
| #19110 | Open | `df.loc[existing_row, new_col] = val` adds a column instead of a (partial) row — missing-label priority is inconsistent with present-label priority |
| #17024 | Open | `df.loc['all'] = [5, 6]` on a MI DataFrame flattens the MI to tupled strings |

### See also

| Issue | Status | Notes |
|-------|--------|-------|
| #39775 | Open | KeyError semantics for partially-missing MI keys in slices — adjacent problem about what should happen when MI keys don't exist |
| #16018 | Closed | `cannot reindex from duplicate axis` on MI expansion (fixed in 1.3) |
| #22247 | Closed | MI expansion with NaN level copies wrong values (fixed) |

## Current behavior

### The resolution rule depends on context

The current code applies different heuristics depending on the operation and key type:

**getitem with scalar tuple** (`_getitem_lowerdim` → `_handle_lowerdim_multi_index_axis0`):
- Try MI key via `obj.xs(tup)`. If found → return row.
- If `KeyError` and `ndim < len(tup) <= nlevels` → re-raise (MI interpretation).
- If `KeyError` and `len(tup) == nlevels == ndim` → raise `IndexingError`, which is suppressed by the caller so the per-axis loop handles it as multi-axis.

This means getitem **silently switches interpretation** when a MI key is missing:

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([(1, 2), (3, 4)])
df = pd.DataFrame([[10, 20], [30, 40]], index=mi, columns=[100, 200])

df.loc[(1, 2)]    # → Series (MI row key found)
df.loc[(1, 100)]  # → Series (MI key not found → silently becomes row=1, col=100)
```

**getitem with slices** (`_getitem_tuple_same_dim`):
- Always multi-axis. `df.loc[:1, 2]` treats `2` as a column, even though `df.loc[1, 2]` treats it as MI level 1 (#16396).

**setitem with scalar tuple** (`_get_setitem_indexer`):
- Try MI key via `ax.get_loc(key)`. If found → overwrite row.
- If `KeyError` → suppress, fall through to `_convert_tuple` (always multi-axis). This is why #27248 fails — the missing MI key is reinterpreted as `(row, new_column)`.

### The result depends on dtype

Because the fallback to multi-axis only triggers when the MI lookup fails, and whether it finds a match depends on what values are in the MI levels, the **same syntax gives different results depending on dtype** (#14969):

```python
# String inner level → (0, 0) is NOT in the MI (level 1 is strings),
# so MI lookup fails and multi-axis takes over: partial level-0 key
# on both axes yields a DataFrame.
ind = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([[0, 1], ['A', 'B']])
df = pd.DataFrame(..., index=ind, columns=ind)
df.loc[0, 0]  # → DataFrame

# Int inner level → (0, 0) IS in the MI, so MI row lookup succeeds
# and returns that single row as a Series (indexed by the column MI).
ind = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([[0, 1], [0, 1]])
df = pd.DataFrame(..., index=ind, columns=ind)
df.loc[0, 0]  # → Series
```

## Cases that already work

The ambiguity only exists when `nlevels == ndim`. These cases work correctly:

- **Series with MI** (`ndim=1`): any tuple with `len > 1` exceeds ndim, so `_convert_tuple` raises `IndexingError("Too many indexers")` and the fallthrough correctly handles MI keys.
- **3+-level MI on DataFrame** (`nlevels > ndim=2`): same mechanism — `_convert_tuple` rejects the tuple and the fallthrough handles it.

## Why heuristics don't work

I explored several heuristic approaches to disambiguate setitem when `nlevels == ndim`:

1. **Check if last element is an existing column**: Fails for `df.loc[partial_key, new_col] = val` (simultaneous row + column expansion).
2. **Check type compatibility of each element with its MI level**: Fails when MI levels and columns share the same dtype (e.g., int/int MI + int columns).
3. **Combined type + column-dtype check**: Handles many cases but is fundamentally a guess — there exist DataFrames where both interpretations are type-valid.

The ambiguity is inherent to the API, not a deficiency in the implementation.

## The right API

I think the right long-term answer is: **`.loc` should not guess**. When `nlevels == ndim`, there should be one canonical interpretation, and the user should use explicit syntax for the other.

### Option A: MI key always wins

`.loc[(a, b)]` on a 2-level MI always means MI row key. Multi-axis indexing requires the explicit `df.loc[(a, b), :]` form (or partial keys like `df.loc[a, col]` when `a` is clearly a single level-0 value).

**Pros**: Consistent with getitem priority (MI key is tried first). Consistent with Series. The multi-axis form `df.loc[..., :]` is explicit and readable.

**Cons**: Behavior change for `df.loc[scalar, col]` when the scalar matches level 0 and `col` matches a column.

### Option B: Multi-axis always wins

`.loc[(a, b)]` on a 2-level MI always means `(row=a, col=b)`. MI row key indexing requires `df.loc[pd.IndexSlice[a, b]]` or `df.loc[(a, b), :]`.

**Pros**: No behavior change for existing multi-axis code. Consistent with how `_convert_tuple` already works.

**Cons**: Breaks `df.loc[(a, b)]` for MI row access, which is arguably the more natural reading. Inconsistent with Series and with the `nlevels > ndim` case.

### Option C: Raise on ambiguity

When `nlevels == ndim` and the key is a plain tuple, raise an error (as suggested in #42603) requiring the user to be explicit. Problem: Python offers no way to distinguish `df.loc[(a, b)]` from `df.loc[a, b]`, so we'd have to reject *all* plain tuple keys when `nlevels == ndim`, which is extremely disruptive.

### My recommendation: Option A

The key observation is that the MI-key interpretation is already the **first thing tried** in both getitem and setitem — the multi-axis path is always a fallback. Making the MI-key interpretation authoritative (rather than a try/except heuristic) would make the behavior predictable and consistent across getitem, setitem, scalars, and slices.

Users who need multi-axis indexing on a 2-level MI DataFrame can write `df.loc[(a, b), :]` or use `pd.IndexSlice`.

## How to get there

1. **Short term**: Document the ambiguity and the `df.loc[(a, b), :]` workaround in the MultiIndex docs.
2. **Medium term**: Add a `FutureWarning` when the ambiguous case is hit — when `nlevels == ndim`, MI key lookup fails, and the code is about to fall back to multi-axis. The warning should suggest explicit syntax.
3. **Long term**: Change the default to MI key interpretation when `nlevels == ndim`, removing the multi-axis fallback.

This would resolve #27248, #19110, #16396, #42603, and #14969. #17024 (MI flattening on scalar expansion) is a separate sub-bug in the expansion machinery.

title: MultiIndex: inconsistent 'mixed depth' squeezing behavior across axes, NA types, and operations
body:
I [the human] asked Claude to post the following:

## Summary

When a DataFrame has MultiIndex columns and a top-level key maps to a single column whose remaining sub-level(s) are all "placeholder" values (empty string `""` or NA), pandas has an undocumented convenience behavior that squeezes the result from a 1-column DataFrame into a Series. This behavior has several inconsistencies:

1. **NaN vs empty string**: `("")` squeezes to Series, but `(NaN)` returns a 1-column DataFrame
2. **Column vs row axis asymmetry**: The squeezing only happens for column indexing (`df["key"]`), not row indexing (`df.loc["key"]`)
3. **How placeholders are created**: `str.split(expand=True)` fills with NaN, `df["newcol"] = ...` fills with `""` — so the same conceptual operation produces different indexing behavior

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("a", ""), ("b", np.nan), ("c", "x"), ("c", "y")])
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(8).reshape(2, 4), columns=idx)

df["a"]  # Series ← squeezes because sub-level is ""
df["b"]  # DataFrame (1 col) ← does NOT squeeze because sub-level is NaN

# Axis asymmetry:
df2 = df.T
df2.loc["a"]  # DataFrame (1 row) ← never squeezes on row axis
df2.T["a"]    # Series ← squeezes on column axis
```

## Related issues

- #11424 — DOC: document level-dropping for empty columns (original report of the undocumented behavior)
- #17024 — `.loc` with partial key flattens MultiIndex on index (scalar labels auto-transformed to `(key, "")` on columns but not rows)
- #17029 — Asymmetric behavior between index and columns when getting incomplete label (the axis asymmetry)
- #25284 — Empty string as sub-index changes the shape (NaN vs `""` inconsistency)
- #25154 — MultiIndex slicing with NaNs, unexpected results (NaN handling in MultiIndex more broadly, now closed)

## Where the behavior lives

The squeezing logic is in `DataFrame._getitem_multilevel` (frame.py, lines 4351-4362):

```python
if len(result.columns) == 1:
    top = result.columns[0]
    if isinstance(top, tuple):
        top = top[0]
    if top == "":
        result = result[""]
        if isinstance(result, Series):
            result = self._constructor_sliced(
                result, index=self.index, name=key
            )
```

Row indexing goes through `NDFrame.xs` → `MultiIndex._get_loc_level`, which has no analogous squeezing.

## Discussion: what is the right API?

There are a few options:

### Option A: Remove the squeezing entirely

`df["key"]` on a MultiIndex always returns a DataFrame, even if there's only one sub-level and it's a placeholder. This is the most predictable behavior — the return type depends only on whether the key is in the top level of a MultiIndex, not on what the sub-level values happen to be.

**Pros:** Simplest, most predictable, eliminates all the inconsistencies at once.
**Cons:** Breaking change for users who rely on the current behavior. The convenience of `df["name"]` returning a Series for "ragged" column structures is real.

### Option B: Extend squeezing to be consistent

Make the squeezing work for all NA-like values (NaN, None, NaT) and on both axes. This means:
- `("key", NaN)` and `("key", "")` both squeeze to Series/scalar on column axis
- `("key", "")` and `("key", NaN)` both squeeze to Series on row axis
- Standardize on a single placeholder value (NaN?) when creating mixed-depth MultiIndexes

**Pros:** Makes the "ragged MultiIndex" use case work consistently.
**Cons:** The squeezing behavior is still magical and undocumented. Return type still depends on sub-level values, not just the structure of the indexing operation.

### Option C: Deprecate squeezing, point users to explicit APIs

Deprecate the squeeze, and recommend users who want a Series from a 1-column sub-selection use `df["key"].squeeze()` or `df[("key", "")]`. Eventually remove the squeezing in a future major version.

**Pros:** Gets to the clean state of Option A without a hard break.
**Cons:** Deprecation period is annoying for users who rely on the current behavior.

title: ENH: `df.duplicated()` default behavior should default to tagging all duplicates as `True`
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Hi, folks. I don't complain much about excellent open-source freeware, and I'm reasonably proficient at Pandas. I have about three years of solid use under my belt; before that, I had about six using Stata and am (was) a Stata maven. Pandas is generally much better...BUT...

`df.duplicated()` has what seems to me to be very confusing default behavior. In Stata, for example, one might use the equivalent duplicate-tagger function (in Stata, a "command") to locate people who are duplicates on a particular column to then hand inspect some of the rows to see if these are data entry errors or if, by contrast, one has perhaps missed a nuance and should expect a small number of duplicates on some col. This might sound sloppy, but when the codebook/docs for the DF sucks, this is a good way to figure out precisely what it might mean for a row to be a duplicate on some subset.

For that reason, I propose that `df.duplicated(keep=False)` should be the default behavior. I just spent around 30 minutes trying to figure out the problem with my code or possibly with the df, etc. because I was trying to locate people who are duplicates on a col that should in theory have a few duplicates but not many, and I could not actually see any duplicates after the following.

```
df["dupe"] = df.duplicated(subset=["year", "id"])
df.groupby("year").apply(lambda g :
    g["df"].mean())
df.loc[df["dupe"]==True].apply(foo)
```

Of course, I realized that this is because the default behavior is to *not* tag the first duplicate as a duplicate; in my case, since the multiplicity of a duplicate is almost always two, that meant that subsetting the data to only include duplicates was actually omitting those duplicates from view.

I did even skim the Docs, obviously inefficiently at first, but the wording *itself* seems extremely confusing. I did not realize that `keep=False` would solve my problems because this is not really about keep/drop behavior but tagging behavior. Changing the option's actual name to `tag` or something similar would probably lead to less confusion/make it more obvious that the default behavior is odd. 

On that note, another reason to change this, I think, is that there is no particular reason to expect the first duplicate to be the one to keep (at least without more context on the df; certainly, this is not true in general). This might make sense if it is a duplicate on all cols, but if the subset is anything but the full set of cols, this seems like behavior that might lead to very unexpected results. If someone does simply have outright duplicate records, it doesn't really cost significant time or memory (AFAICT) to then go back and set `keep="first"` once it's been confirmed that one might as well keep any record.

### Feature Description

I'm not a backend dev., merely a fairly tech-savvy sociologist. I think the technical side of this would be very easy.

### Alternative Solutions

People could read the docs very carefully before seeking other solutions.

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: BUG: DataFrame/Series.rename silently downcasts nullable index/column dtypes to NumPy dtypes
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
      {"val": [1, 2, 3]},
      index=pd.Index(pd.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="Int64"), name="id"),
  )
print(df.index.dtype)
print(df.rename({1: 9}).index.dtype)
```

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.rename()` and `Series.rename()` do not preserve nullable extension dtypes on index/column labels. In the reproduced cases with nullable integer and floating dtypes, renaming labels silently downcasts the result to the corresponding NumPy dtype.

The root cause appears to be `Index._transform_index()`, which reconstructs the transformed index from a plain Python list instead of preserving/casting through the original `ExtensionArray` dtype.

title: ENH: pd.crosstab with normalize='index' and margins=True drops the marginal 'Total' column.
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

When creating a contingency table using pd.crosstab, if a user specifies normalize='index' while also requesting margins=True, the resulting DataFrame includes the marginal row (at the bottom) but excludes the marginal column (on the right). While the marginal column would mathematically consist of constants (1.0), its omission prevents the generation of a complete "framed" table for reporting and visualization purposes.

It is normal in data science to display both row and column totals in a crosstab.  If you select row or column as the sum, it's expect to show 100% on the non-selected column,  this is supported by the grand total selection where only the total in the bottom right is 100%.  This helps users quick understand what you are trying to convey and reinforces the choice of display 

The default should be to hide the result which is 1.0

### Feature Description

def _add_margins(self, table, margins_name):
    # CURRENT BEHAVIOR: 
    # Pandas calculates the sum of columns and rows.
    # If normalize='index', the row sum is always 1.0.
    
    # PROPOSED FIX:
    # Explicitly check if normalize is 'index' or 'columns' 
    # to prevent the 'Total' column/row from being optimized away.

    if self.normalize == 'index':
        # Force add the marginal column of 1.0s
        table[margins_name] = 1.0 
        
        # Calculate the marginal row (the distribution of the columns)
        # This is the mean of the normalized rows or a separate total calculation
        column_totals = table.iloc[:, :-1].mean(axis=0) 
        table.loc[margins_name] = column_totals
        table.at[margins_name, margins_name] = 1.0
        
    return table

title: BUG: read_csv() into FloatingArrays converts np.nan into pd.NA, even with distinguish_nan_and_na=True
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

csv = """,x
a,1.0
b,
c,nan"""

with pd.option_context("future.distinguish_nan_and_na", True):
    s = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), index_col=0, dtype={0: str, 1: pd.Float64Dtype()},
                     keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])["x"]
s
```

### Issue Description

Working with data having both `pd.NA` and `np.nan` is possible and, at least until pandas2, it was possible to save such dataframes as CSV in a format that keeps a distinction between the two (see #65227).

However, in the example above pandas fails with:

```
ValueError: Unable to parse string "nan" at position 2
```

The current workaround consists in reading the CSV as string, and manually map its value to floats:
```python
import io
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

csv = """,x
a,1.0
b,
c,nan"""


def convert_nan(val: str):
    match val:
        case "":
            return pd.NA
        case _:
            return np.float64(val) # includes np.nan

with pd.option_context("future.distinguish_nan_and_na", True):
    s1 = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), index_col=0, dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)["x"]
    s2 = s1.map(convert_nan)
    s3 = s2.convert_dtypes()
s1,s2,s3
```
returns:
```
(a    1.0
 b       
 c    nan
 Name: x, dtype: str,
 a     1.0
 b    <NA>
 c     NaN
 Name: x, dtype: object,
 a     1.0
 b    <NA>
 c     NaN
 Name: x, dtype: Float64)
```

### Expected Behavior

I would expect `read_csv()` to distinguish between `NA` and `NaN` in the columns with `dtype=Float64`. Even more so if `distinguish_nan_and_na=True`.
```
 a     1.0
 b    <NA>
 c     NaN
 Name: x, dtype: Float64
```

title: BUG: [REGRESSION] to_csv cannot handle FloatingArrays with np.nan, even with distinguish_nan_and_na=True
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series((1, pd.NA, 0), index=["a","b","c"], dtype=pd.Float64Dtype(), name="x")
with pd.option_context("future.distinguish_nan_and_na", True):
    s = s/s # creates a series with both NA and NaN
    print(s.to_csv(sep=",", mode="w"))
```

### Issue Description

The above code raises the following error:
```
ArrowTypeError: Expected bytes, got a 'numpy.float64' object
```

A similar code, worked as expected with Pandas<3 (i.e. `pandas=2.3.2`, with `PyArrow=21.0.0` just like for pandas3):
```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series((1, pd.NA, 0), index=["a","b","c"], dtype=pd.Float64Dtype(), name="x")
s = s/s # creates a series with both NA and NaN
print(s.to_csv(sep=",", mode="w"))
```
prints: 
```
,x
a,1.0
b,
c,nan
```

### Expected Behavior

I would expect to have the same behaviour as Pandas2. Even more so if `distinguish_nan_and_na=True`.

Note that Pandas2 distinguished between NA and NaN (i.e. empty string vs `"nan"` string)

title: CI regression: Doc Build and pre-commit jobs failing across multiple PRs
body:
### Describe the bug

The following CI jobs are failing across multiple unrelated PRs:

- Doc Build and Upload
- Code Checks / Docstring validation, typing, and other manual pre-commit hooks

Failures appear unrelated to PR contents and occur during environment setup/build.

---

### Evidence

Observed failures on:

- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65212
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65224
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65225

All show failures in:

- Doc Build and Upload
- Docstring validation, typing, and other manual pre-commit hooks
